cd1.name: Boots for the Wall

objective.label: Deliver the muster sheets to the four watch posts in order, from the Harbour Tower on the south mole up to the Crown Terrace

cd1.desc: Gate-Sergeant Ottey of the Drill Yards wants a newcomer to carry the night's four muster sheets along Caerdun's wall, one to each watch post in order: the Harbour Tower, the Lighthouse, the Sea Ramparts and the Crown Terrace. Then report back to Ottey.
offer: You. Yes, you, with the face. Gate-Sergeant Ottey, of the Drill Yards; I keep the watch rota for the whole wall, which tonight means I have four muster sheets and nobody with working knees to carry them. Can you walk and hold paper at the same time? Don't answer, it was a test, you passed by not answering.

Here is what you need to know about this city before you walk its wall. Three hundred years ago the Empire of Vanai emptied itself in one night and shut its border behind it. We were its border garrison, posted out here on the fjord, and the door shut with us on the outside. The empire left us on the step like a delivery nobody signed for. Fine. We're Caerdun. We signed for ourselves.

So the wall gets walked every night, and every post on it hands in a muster sheet, the night's watch rota, so the paymaster can write down who stood where. Up here we don't ask why we still keep the watch. It has been kept every night for three hundred years, and it will not stop being kept because my knees have opinions.

Take these four sheets. Walk the wall from the harbour up to the crown and hand one in at each watch post, in this order. First, the Harbour Tower Watch, out at the end of the south mole; mind the fish carts on the quay, they yield for no one. Second, the Lighthouse Watch, at the lighthouse's foot: Lamp-Keeper Hilde Varn is deaf in her right ear, so stand on her left or you'll say everything twice.

Third, the Sea Ramparts Watch, up on the sea wall. Fourth and last, the Crown Terrace Watch, the highest post in the city. My father held that post. His father before him. Then come back down to me at the Drill Yards and I'll see you're entered as having walked it. There's a pair of Traveler's Boots in it for you; nobody walks my wall in whatever you've got on.

When I was small I asked my grandmother what we were watching for, and she said: the day the question answers itself. For most of my life I took that as her way of saying she didn't know. Lately I'm less sure.
progress: Four sheets, four posts, in order: the Harbour Tower Watch at the end of the south mole, the Lighthouse Watch at the tower's foot (stand on Hilde Varn's left), the Sea Ramparts Watch on the sea wall, and the Crown Terrace Watch at the top. Then back to me at the Drill Yards.
complete: All four signed for? Good. You've walked the wall; that is what this city is, and now you're part of it. Small problem. The tally came back from the posts tonight and your name's not in the book, because nobody has entered you yet. Things that aren't in the book upset people. Specifically one person.

Paymaster Vail. She keeps the Wage Vaults, under the court hall: the room where every night of watch this garrison has ever stood is written down and valued, and she'll want your name in it properly before you stand another. Go and upset her in person. Walk slow. Build your courage. She has never once been surprised, and I'd not want to be the one who starts.
And here: the boots. Wear them. The wall's a long walk, and you'll be walking it again.

cd2.name: The Book of Debts

objective.label: Fetch the three archive volumes from the deep vault: year one, year one-fifty, year three hundred

cd2.desc: Paymaster Vail will not enter your name in Caerdun's wage book until its chain of volumes is verified back to the first page. Fetch three archive volumes from the deep vault below the Wage Vaults: Year One, Year One Hundred and Fifty and Year Three Hundred.
offer: Name. Spell it. No: spell it the way you'll spell it for the rest of your life, because once it's in this book, that is who you are. I am Paymaster Vail. Ottey sent you down because you walked the wall last night and nobody had entered you. That is Ottey's fault, and now it is my problem.

You should understand what this room is before your name goes in it. The empire left on one night three hundred years ago; Caerdun calls that night the Sealing, because the border shut and the garrison was on the wrong side of it. It left without paying its garrison. So we kept the invoice. Nine generations of my family have kept this room, and in it every night of watch stood on that wall since the Sealing is written down, valued and owed.

Volume one, page one, the night watch of the night itself, reads: one night: owed. Whoever wrote that had just watched an empire vanish, and their hand didn't shake. Three hundred volumes later the book is still kept the same way, and last night's watch, yours, will go in exactly as that one did.

The rule is this: no name enters the book until the chain of volumes is verified, every volume initialled back to that first page, and the newest name does the fetching. That is you. Go down into the deep vault below this room; the volumes stand on shelves on rails. Bring me three: the Archive Volume for Year One, the one for Year One Hundred and Fifty, and the one for Year Three Hundred, this year's. I'll take them in that order and check the initials across them.

Touch nothing else down there. The vault notices. Bring the three to this desk and I'll verify the chain, enter your name, and pay you two Potions for the carrying, out of the garrison's own stores, since nobody else is paying us.
progress: Three volumes from the deep vault below this room, off the shelves on rails: Year One, Year One Hundred and Fifty, Year Three Hundred. Bring them to my desk in that order, and touch nothing else down there.
complete: One. One-fifty. Three hundred. The initials run true across all three; the chain holds, and your name goes in. Spell it once more. Good. You are in the book now, which means the empire owes you for last night, along with everyone else in this city.

Hold. There is a page in volume three hundred that does not belong in it. It is misfiled: wrong century, wrong hand, wrong paper. This is not Caerdun's paper and this is not a Caerdun hand. And the seal pressed at the bottom... I have read every seal this city has ever pressed, every court, every guild, every family, and I do not know this one.

I will not guess at it, and I will not have it in my vault unaccounted for. Take the page to Marshal Grett, who commands the Drill Yards and holds the garrison's oath. If anyone in Caerdun will admit to recognising a seal like that, it is a woman with nothing left to be afraid of. Tell her I sent it, and tell her exactly where it was found: between the pages of this year's volume, in my own vault.

cd3.name: Hold Until Relieved

objective.label: Kill 6 grey wolves raiding the watch farms in the Caerdun Fields

cd3.desc: Marshal Grett knows the strange seal on the misfiled page but has sworn to tell no civilian. To be sworn in as a soldier of Caerdun, defeat 6 Grey Wolves raiding the Watch Farms in the Caerdun Fields, south of the road out of the Landward Gate, then return to her at the Drill Yards.
offer: Vail sent you? Then stand there and don't die of anything while I finish this drill. FORMS! Wall-form third! Your grandmothers held this line with worse knees and better attitudes! ...Right. Marshal Grett. I command these yards and I hold the garrison's oath, and I can see from here that you're wondering why we still drill wall-forms against an enemy that has not come in three hundred years.

Because our oath isn't fight. Our oath is hold until relieved. A relief is the company that comes to take over your post so you can stand down. Nobody relieved us. The empire shut the border and never sent one. So we hold. By my count that is roughly one hundred and nine thousand shifts past due, and you may inform the empire of that whenever it gets home.

Now. Your page, with the seal. Yes, I saw it when you came in, and yes, I know it. What I know about that seal I swore an oath to keep, and I don't break oaths for civilians. So: stop being one. I can swear in a recruit who has stood a shift for this garrison. Stand one, and we talk as soldiers.

Tonight's shift is this. Grey wolves have come down on the Watch Farms, the garrison's own farms out in the Caerdun Fields; they're taking lambs from the pens and the farmers have had enough. Go out through the Landward Gate, the city's east gate, and follow the road into the Fields; the farms lie south of the road. Kill the wolves raiding the pens, the bold ones, six at least.

Then come back to me here at the Drill Yards. You take the oath, I hand you a sword worth the name, a Bronze Sword from the garrison armoury, and I tell you what that seal is. Not before, child. Not before.
progress: The Grey Wolves are at the Watch Farms, south of the road in the Caerdun Fields, out through the Landward Gate. Six of them dead, then back to me at the Drill Yards for the oath.
complete: Six wolves. The farmers will sleep tonight, and so will the lambs. Decent work. Raise your hand and say it: hold until relieved. You've said it, you're sworn, and you're a soldier of Caerdun. Now I can talk.

The seal. Every marshal of this garrison learns it once, from a book we keep locked, and swears never to describe it to anyone who hasn't taken the oath. It is the personal seal of the imperial paymaster-general: the officer of the empire whose job it was to pay the garrison. The office that would pay us. That seal has not been pressed on this side of the border since the Sealing.

Think about what you carried in here. That page was written on paper we haven't milled in three centuries, by a hand none of us knows, under the seal of the empire's paymaster, and it was filed into our vault, between this year's pages, by someone. Documents like that come from one place, child. Inside the border. Where nothing comes from.

I don't know what it means yet, and I don't like not knowing. Keep the page; you're sworn to it now. Duelist-Master Sabel wants you; she's here at the Drill Yards too, on the far side of the yard by the granite ring. Something about a duel, and she asked for you. Go and see what she wants.

cd4.name: A Duel Before Witnesses

objective.label: Stand second to Sabel at the Harrow-Tallis duel on the Dueling Ground in the Drill Yards

cd4.desc: Duelist-Master Sabel needs a second with no stake in the quarrel for a duel between the Harrow and Tallis families at the Dueling Ground in Caerdun's Drill Yards. The real quarrel is an imperial wage schedule the Tallis boy found, which the Harrows want burned.
offer: Ah, the paymaster's new favourite, and Grett's newest sworn blade. I'm Duelist-Master Sabel; I keep the duelling code for this city, which means that when two families fall out over something the court can't settle, they settle it in front of me, under rules, instead of in an alley. Perfect timing. I need a second for a duel this afternoon.

The code requires that a second has no stake in the quarrel: no kin on either side, no debt, no grudge. Everyone born in Caerdun is somebody's cousin. You are the only sworn blade in this city with no cousin, no debt and no grudge on either side of this one. Being new is finally worth something.

The quarrel, as the families tell it: the Harrows and the Tallises have a dispute over an old wage claim and are settling it the old way. One duelist for each family, first blood ends it, every grievance between the families discharged on the spot, drinks after. It keeps the lawyers poor, which I consider a public service.

The quarrel, as it actually is: quietly, now. Young Tallis found a paper in his grandmother's chest, an imperial wage schedule, a paymaster's list of what the empire paid Caerdun's garrison and when. The Harrows want it burned, and they are frightened enough to bleed for it. People don't fight over old paper. They fight over paper that frightens them. The duel is theatre. Watch the families, not the blades.

Your office is simple. Walk to the Dueling Ground, the ring of worn granite here in the Drill Yards, where both families will be waiting. Stand at my left through the forms and keep your hands in sight. If anyone who is not a duelist draws steel, put yourself in the way; that is what a second is for. That, and looking composed. Practise on the walk over. There's a Wayfarer Vest in the code's chest for a second who does the office properly.
progress: The Dueling Ground, the granite ring here in the Drill Yards. Stand at my left through the forms, watch the families rather than the blades, and if anyone who isn't a duelist draws, get in the way.
complete: First blood, honour served, and nobody's cousin started a war. You saw the Harrow cousin go for his knife when the Tallis blade landed; your shoulder was in his way before mine was. That's the office. The vest is yours.

And here is what the afternoon was really about. The Tallis boy gave me the schedule the moment the drinks came out; he was glad to be rid of it, and I don't blame him. It's a wage schedule from the imperial paymaster's office: the garrison's pay, year by year, with the date each payment falls due. Look at the dates. Run your finger down the column.

They don't stop at the Sealing. The empire vanished three hundred years ago, and this list of payments to its garrison keeps going. Right through us: through every year since, through this year. Somebody drew up a schedule for paying a garrison across three centuries in which they weren't here to pay it.

I'm a duelist, not a clerk; I know what frightens a Harrow, not what a column of dates means. Vail does. Take the schedule to Paymaster Vail in the Wage Vaults under the court hall and lay it beside her misfiled page. Then watch a woman who has never once been surprised, and see what she does.

cd5.name: The Last Payday

objective.label: Climb the clock tower beside the court hall and copy the Sealed Imperial Clock's count through the grate, touching nothing

cd5.desc: The imperial wage schedule is genuine, and its final entry is a settlement in full of every night of watch since the Sealing, on one date that is close. Paymaster Vail wants that date checked against the Sealed Imperial Clock in the clock tower beside the court hall: copy its count through the grate, touching nothing.
offer: Close the door. Sit. I have been at this desk with the Tallis schedule since you brought it down yesterday, and I want a witness with fresh eyes before I say any of this aloud.

The schedule is genuine. It came from the imperial paymaster's office: correct forms, correct arithmetic, and the paymaster-general's seal, the same seal as the page you found misfiled in my vault. It lists the wages of Caerdun's garrison, paid in advance, year over year, for three hundred years: every year of our watch, entered on their books before we had stood a night of it, in a book we had never seen. And then it does something no ledger in this room has ever done.

Let me tell you what three hundred years sounds like in a book, so you understand what that schedule is matched against. Year forty-one: the winter of the long ice; double shifts, every one written. Year one hundred and twelve: plague on the harbour terrace; eleven names struck, and the watch stood regardless. Year two hundred and six: my great-great-grandmother's hand takes over mid-page, because the paymaster before her died at this desk. We ruled a line and kept going.

I always believed we kept this book to hold a grudge. We did not. We were keeping faith, and we didn't even know it. Because the schedule ends. Not stops: ends. Its final entry reads: settlement in full, all garrison wages, every night of watch since the Sealing. One payment. One date.

Debts get settled when the debtor plans to be in the room. Someone, three hundred years ago, wrote down the day they intend to walk in here and pay us. And the date is close. Not years off. Months, by my reading.

I need the date checked against the only imperial thing in this city that still runs. The clock tower beside the court hall holds an imperial clock, sealed behind a grate below the bell floor; it has kept its own count since before the Sealing, and nobody has ever been able to stop it or set it. Climb the tower, read the dial-count through the grate, copy the numbers exactly, touch nothing, and bring them straight back to this desk. Two Hi-Potions for the climb; the stair is older than the city.
progress: The clock tower beside the court hall. Climb to the grate below the bell floor, copy the Sealed Imperial Clock's dial-count exactly, touch nothing, and bring the numbers back to my desk in the Wage Vaults.
complete: Read them to me. ...Again. The clock's count agrees with the schedule, to the day. Of course it agrees; it's theirs. The same hands that set that clock drew up this schedule, and both of them point at one morning.

Three hundred years I believed my family kept this book so that the dead could sue. A grudge, bound in leather. We were wrong. We kept it because the empire intends to pay: someone means to walk into this vault on the day they fixed, and they left a clock running in our tower, counting to it. Every night we wrote down, they had already written down first.

I need to sit down. I am sitting down. This is past a paymaster now. The Lord Marshal must hear it tonight; he is Caerdun's ruler, and he keeps to the Parade Square, between the Paladin Hall and the Duelling Code. Take him my report and the schedule, and tell him Vail sent you with both. Tell him the date is close. He will want to read it three times. Let him.

cd6.name: Word to the Inn

objective.label: Ride east across the Caerdun Fields, take the North Road at Milestone Zero, and ask Auntie Wren at the Halfway Inn for the long table

cd6.desc: Caerdun holds one piece of the mystery: a date on which the empire means to pay its garrison in full. The Lord Marshal names you Caerdun's envoy. Ride east across the Caerdun Fields, take the North Road at Milestone Zero, and ask Auntie Wren at the Halfway Inn for the long table.
offer: So you're the one Vail sent. I am the Lord Marshal; I rule Caerdun, such as ruling it is, and I've read Vail's report three times: once as a soldier, once as a ruler, once as a man whose grandfather died on that wall. It reads differently each time and it never reads well.

Let me say plainly what we now know. The empire paid our garrison in advance for three hundred years. Its schedule ends in one settlement in full, on one date, and the clock it left in our tower is counting to that same date, which by Vail's reckoning is soon. Someone on the far side of that border means to walk into our vault and pay us. That is Caerdun's corner of this: a payment date. But a date for what? Payment, yes. And what else walks in through the door with the paymaster?

We are not the only city holding a piece. Heartwood, over the mountains to the east, keeps a song no one is allowed to finish; its singers have passed the verses down for three centuries and fine anyone who hums the end. Moonmere, the academy on its island across the gulf, sealed a room the week the empire vanished and has lied about it, politely, ever since. Three cities, three pieces, three centuries of not comparing notes. That ends now.

The three cities have agreed to meet at the Halfway Inn on the North Road, because it sits on neither city's ground. You go as Caerdun's envoy, carrying its evidence: you found the misfiled page, you carried the schedule, you climbed to the clock. An envoy who can say I saw it myself is worth ten who can only say I was told. And Vail vouched for you, and Vail has never vouched for anything, including sunrise.

The road: go out through the Landward Gate and ride east across the Caerdun Fields to Milestone Zero, the stone every imperial road was measured from. Take the North Road there, and stay on the road through the snow until you reach the Halfway Inn. Ask Auntie Wren for the long table and tell her you're Caerdun's. Take your winter coat. Take two.

Carry Vail's report and the schedule, and carry this from me: the title Envoy of Caerdun, an Iron Longsword from the garrison's own racks, and a Remedy for the cold. If the empire truly means to settle its debts, what begins at that table is the largest transaction in the history of the world. Try to be worth witnessing.
progress: Out the Landward Gate, east across the Caerdun Fields to Milestone Zero, then the North Road through the snow to the Halfway Inn. Ask Auntie Wren for the long table and say you're Caerdun's.
complete: Stamp your boots, love, the snow comes in with you or it doesn't come in at all. Caerdun, by the coat; I'd know that garrison grey in the dark. I'm Wren, Auntie Wren to everyone who has ever eaten here, and this is the Halfway Inn, the one lit window between your city and Heartwood. You'll be wanting the long table. It's by the fire; I've kept it clear all day.

Sit yourself down and I'll bring stew before anyone says a word about empires. Whatever you've carried over those mountains, it'll keep until you've eaten; things usually do. And you may as well know now, before you reach the fire: you're not the only one who's come with a story tonight. There are others at the table already, from further off than you, and more expected before the night's out.

hw1.name: Learn the Refrain

objective.label: Gather 5 windfall apples from the ground of the wild orchards in the Heartwood Fields

hw1.desc: Chanter Ives, who teaches on the Song-Steps in Heartwood, wants a newcomer's first gift for the ring: five windfall apples from the ground of the wild orchards in the Heartwood Fields, brought back to the Song-Steps and set down while you sing the four-line greeting-song where the old trees can hear.
offer: Stop slouching, you'll dent the note before you've sung it. I'm Chanter Ives; I teach the songs on these steps, the Song-Steps, and I have been short of new voices all week. You're new, so here is the first thing everyone in Heartwood learns: the greeting-song. Four lines, older than the wall at the west pass. It's how the trees know you're not a stranger. Don't laugh. The trees fined a man last spring. Well. We fined him. On their behalf.

Understand the city before you sing to it. Heartwood keeps everything in songs: law, land, grudges, recipes. Paper burns and stone gets carted off by empires, but a song lives in too many chests to steal. So when a Heartwood voice sings the greeting, it is saying: I know what this place keeps, and I will keep it too.

Now, the ring. That is the Grove Ring at the heart of the city: the four great elder trees, and the council of families that sits under them and decides for Heartwood. The ring has not met you. A newcomer introduces themselves properly: you bring the orchard's windfall as a first gift, and you sing the greeting where the old trees can hear. Do that, and every door and every verse in Heartwood opens easier to a voice the grove knows.

Here is the errand. Take this basket west out of the West Gate into the Heartwood Fields. North of the crossroads you'll find the wild orchards. Gather five windfall apples from the ground under the trees: fallen fruit only, never picked. Picked fruit is taking; windfall is given. Fill the basket and bring it back to me here on the Song-Steps.

When you set the basket down, sing the greeting. I'll teach you the four lines now; you'll have them by the time you reach the gate. I receive the gift on the ring's behalf. Sing loudly. The trees are old and so is their hearing, probably. For your trouble there's a pair of boots that will stand up to the Fields better than those.
progress: Five windfall apples, from the ground, never picked. The wild orchards are west through the West Gate into the Heartwood Fields, north of the crossroads. Bring the full basket back to me on the Song-Steps and sing the greeting as you set it down.
complete: Set it down. Now sing. ...Not terrible. You held the third line a shade long, but the ring didn't shudder, and I have heard the ring shudder. The gift is received: five windfall apples from the wild orchards, given by a new voice, and the trees have heard you say who you are. From today every door in Heartwood, and every verse we keep, opens a little easier to you. You're ready for real verses.

Which brings me to Petta. Orchardist Petta keeps the wild orchards you just walked, out in the Heartwood Fields north of the crossroads; she prunes every tree in them and will tell you so. Go back out and see her. She has something she badly wants asked about, and she can't ask it herself without paying a fine.

One warning, and I mean it kindly. If you hear her humming something that stops in the middle, be polite and pretend you didn't. In this city there are songs you can be fined for finishing, and Petta hums very close to the edge of one.

hw2.name: The Banned Song

objective.label: Ask Elder Hazel, Old Tammon and the Widow Crake, in the Heartwood Fields, each for their family's verse of the counting-song

elder_hazel: Petta's itch, is it? She's sent you to ask for the Hazel verse of the counting-song. Sit. You don't get the verse standing up; that's not how it was given to me.

I was seven. My grandmother took me out to the winter orchard at midnight and sang it once, into my ear, with her hands over mine like the words might spill. Nine for the lamps they left alight. Then she said: you'll sing this to one child, once, and you'll know when. I have been holding it sixty years, waiting to know when. Come closer, then. Once.
old_tammon: Petta sent you for the Tammon verse? Then sit on the stool by the brook and listen to the water first. The verse goes with the sound of the wheel; it was made to. Six for the wheel that turns for none.
My father sang it to me on this stool, and his father sang it to him. Nobody sings it right who hasn't sat where you're sitting. Now you have. Take it to Petta.
widow_crake: From up here you can see the whole of the Fields and none of the Estates, the empire's timber plantations over the border, where our groves used to be. That is by design. Mine. Sit; the wind's less if you're low. You've come for the Crake verse.

Eleven for the doors we did not lock. My mother gave me that one the morning the Border Gate at the west end of these Fields first ticked, the way a clock ticks, with nobody near it. She said I'd know what the verse meant when I heard the rest of the song. I never did hear the rest. Perhaps you will.

hw2.desc: Orchardist Petta in the wild orchards wants the counting-song finished, which Heartwood forbids, so a newcomer must ask for her. Ask Elder Hazel at her orchard gate, Old Tammon by the mill brook and the Widow Crake on the ridge path, all in the Heartwood Fields, each for their family's verse, then bring the verses back to Petta.
offer: ...four for the gates that shut so soft... oh! You heard nothing. That's a fining offence, what you didn't hear. I'm Petta; I keep these orchards. Wild, they call them; I prune every one. And you're the new voice Ives has been teaching the greeting to. Good. I need a new voice.

Since you're already an accomplice, I'll tell you what you didn't hear. It's the counting-song. The oldest song Heartwood has. Every child in this city knows how it starts, and no one alive knows how it ends, because finishing it is forbidden. A song we made ourselves and then banned ourselves from singing. Doesn't that itch at you? It itches at me. It has itched at me for thirty years.

Here is how they did it. When the song was banned, the verses were scattered on purpose, one to a family, so that no single mouth could ever finish it by accident. Three of the elder families out here in the Fields hold a verse each. If I go asking, every elder knows exactly what I'm assembling and I'm fined into next winter. But a newcomer, fresh from singing the greeting, asking sweetly about the old songs? That's just education. Nobody fines education.

So you'll ask for me. Three people, all here in the Heartwood Fields. Elder Hazel, at her orchard gate. Old Tammon, by the brook beside the mill. The Widow Crake, up on the ridge path to the west. Ask each of them for their family's verse of the counting-song.

Two things to remember. Sit when they tell you to sit; the verses come with furniture, each one was given sitting down and that's how they give it on. And tell them Petta says the itch has got worse. They'll know what it means. Bring all three verses back to me here in the orchards and I'll set them next to mine, and we'll see what this song has been counting.
progress: Three verses, from three people in the Heartwood Fields: Elder Hazel at her orchard gate, Old Tammon by the brook beside the mill, and the Widow Crake on the ridge path to the west. Sit when they say sit. Then come back to me in the wild orchards.
complete: Give them here. Hazel's, Tammon's, Crake's. Now listen to them next to mine, and next to the start every child knows. One for the year the ships went still. Two for the wall through the timber hill. Four for the gates that shut so soft. Six for the wheel that turns for none. Nine for the lamps they left alight. Eleven for the doors we did not lock.

Do you hear it? It isn't a nursery rhyme. It's a count. One verse for each year since the night the empire vanished, each year told by something that happened in it: the ships going still, the wall going up through the timber hill, the gates shutting so soft. Heartwood has been counting the years since they left, and hiding the count from itself.

And here is what has stopped my breath. It's three hundred years this year since the Night, and the song doesn't stop at this year. It keeps going. There are verses for years that haven't happened yet. Somebody counted past us, child, and then made very sure we would keep saying the words.

That's not an orchardist's business any more. It's the grudge hall's. Grudge-Keeper Morrow keeps the hall in Heartwood where everything the empire took from us is written down, every grove and every family; if anyone can say what the empire meant by a count, it's her. Go back into the city, find the Grudge Hall, and tell Morrow what you've heard. Tell her Petta sent you, and that I'll pay the fine.

hw3.name: The Grudge Hall

objective.label: Recover 4 grave-goods from the barrow diggers' setts in the west of the Heartwood Fields

hw3.desc: Grudge-Keeper Morrow of the Grudge Hall wants the displaced families' grave-goods back before the families visit on Thursday: badger-like barrow diggers are digging up the old graves in the west of the Heartwood Fields, past the charcoal camps under the ridge, and carrying the goods underground. Defeat them and recover four pieces.
offer: Welcome to the grudge hall. Wipe your feet; the floor is grudges. I'm Morrow, the grudge-keeper; I keep the floor. Everything the empire took from Heartwood is written in this room: every grove felled to plant their Timber Estates, every family moved at pike-point to make room for their King's Gardens, the emperor's pleasure grounds over the border, who, when, and how many acres. People call us bitter. We prefer accurate.

Petta sent you, and sent word ahead of you. A song that counts the years, and counts past today. I've read it into the book; it will keep. The counting-song is Heartwood's grievance set to a tune, and a grievance with a date in it is a different animal from a grievance without. But before I say another word about dates, the hall has today's business, and you're going to do it.

Here is what's wrong. The families the empire displaced buried their dead out in the Heartwood Fields, in the old plots west of the city. Something is digging those graves up and carrying the grave-goods underground: the cups, the rings, the keepsakes people were buried with. Badger creatures, big ones. The orchard children call them barrow diggers, as if naming a thing settled it. Grief, hoarded, in a hole.

I'd go myself, but the last time I attended a grave-robbery in person the hall gained three new pages, and I'm told they were all about me. So. The barrow diggers have dug in west of the Fields, past the charcoal camps, under the ridge. Go out there, defeat the diggers, and take back the grave-goods they carry. Four pieces will account for this week's lot. Bring every piece here to me.

Why it can't wait: the displaced families visit this hall on Thursday, to stand on the page that records what was taken from them. They will want their dead's goods back in the ground before then, and so do I. Do this and I'll show you the page this whole hall was built on. There's a pair of wraps in it for your hands, too; the diggers bite.
progress: Four grave-goods. The barrow diggers carry them; they've dug in west in the Heartwood Fields, past the charcoal camps, under the ridge. Defeat them, take back every piece, and bring it all to me at the grudge hall before Thursday.
complete: Four pieces. Cups, a ring, a child's token. Every one back where it belongs, and the families will find their dead undisturbed on Thursday. Good. The hall will note that it was done, and by whom. Now, since you've earned a look: this is the founding page of the grudge hall, the first thing ever written on this floor.

It's the empire's own writ of compensation: the paper they gave Heartwood when they took the groves, an admission that they took them and a promise to pay for them. Read the terms. 'Restitution upon Return.' Payment when they come back. Note the capital letter on Return. The empire didn't write that word the way you'd write it for a cart coming home. They wrote it like the name of a day.

For three hundred years we read that as religion, some notion of a paradise where accounts get settled. But grudge-keepers don't do religion, friend. We do appointments. A date, a debtor, a sum. And Petta's count says the song keeps counting past today. Put the two side by side and it reads like this: the empire took our groves and promised to pay when it came back, and our own counting-song keeps count past today, toward a day that hasn't come yet. It seems we have an appointment.

I don't like how neatly that fits. I've written it down anyway. The Speaker of the Ring will want to hear it from you: that's Heartwood's ruler, the one who speaks for the ring of families and sits under the four great elders in the Grove Ring at the heart of the city. Go to the ring and tell the Speaker what you've carried from Petta and from me. I'll be here, with the book.

hw4.name: Ring Count

objective.label: Mark the four mourning elders' tally posts sunwise: north, east, south, west; return to the Speaker

hw4.desc: The Speaker of the Ring wants an unimpeachable tally of the four mourning elder trees of the Grove Ring, which are all budding at once for the first time in three hundred years: mark the tally post at each tree sunwise, north, east, south, west, and bring the board back to the Speaker under the ring.
offer: You've been busy in my city. Verses from the Fields, grudges from the hall, questions everywhere. Good. I am the Speaker of the Ring; I speak for the families who sit in council under these trees. Sit under the ring with me a moment. It's rude to talk about the trees where they can't hear.

These four great trees, the elders, were planted the night the empire vanished. One at each quarter: north, east, south, west. Mourning trees, the story goes. But look at them properly. They're imperial stock. Bred, not wild; you can tell by the bark and by the way the branches are set. Bred trees are bred for something.

I'll tell you what this variety is bred for, because the ring has always known it and never said it aloud. It flowers exactly once in its life, at full maturity, and every tree of the kind flowers together, in the same week. For three hundred years not one of these four has carried a flower.

Look up. There, on the low boughs. Buds opening into pale flowers. Every tree, all at once, this week. Whoever set these four in the ground planted trees that would flower together three hundred years off, and that time is nearly here. Someone planted us a clock, child, and it is striking.

The families will want to disbelieve it. So the tally must be unimpeachable: every tree walked and marked by eyes that belong to no Heartwood family and owe no verse. Yours. Take this tally-board. Start at the North Elder's Tally Post, at the foot of the north tree, and walk the ring sunwise, the way the sun goes: north, east, south, west. At each post, look up at the tree and mark the board. Bring me the board when the circle closes. There's a robe for the work, woven here.
progress: Four tally posts, one at the foot of each elder tree of the Grove Ring, marked sunwise in order: the North Elder's, then the East, the South, the West. Look up at each tree, mark the board, then bring the board back to me under the ring.
complete: All four. North, east, south, west, every elder in the ring in bud at once, marked by a hand no family can accuse. Give me the board. Now I'll tell you what the board means, because I can read it against something you've already carried into this city.

The count matches the counting-song. The years the song counts, from the night the empire vanished to the verses that run past us, and the years these trees have taken to come to flower: verse for verse, they agree. The song and the trees are counting toward the same morning. Yes, I know the song. I'm the Speaker. Banning a thing means keeping a copy, and the Speaker keeps the copy.

There is one verse left that nobody in this city has heard sung in sixty years, the last one, and there is one voice entitled to sing it. The ring has decided, this minute, with me as its only member present, that it is time we heard the end. Go to Chanter Ives on the Song-Steps and say the Speaker says: finish the song. Ives will know what to do, and who to ask.

hw5.name: Finish the Song

objective.label: Invite the Speaker, Morrow, Petta, Hazel, Tammon and Crake, then return to Ives at the Song-Steps

speaker_of_the_ring: A full ring, when Ives calls, to hear the last verse. I've waited my whole tenure to be summoned to my own trees. Tell Ives the Speaker will come, and will sit where the Speaker has always sat.
grudgekeeper_morrow_hw: Strictly, I wasn't invited. The law of the last verse calls the families, and the grudge hall is not a family; Ives sent you because Ives knows I'd come anyway. Grudges are a kind of song; I keep the ones nobody wants to sing. Tell Ives I'll be at the Song-Steps. I'll stand at the back, lawfully, and I'm bringing ink: whatever that verse says, the hall will have it written down before the tea is poured.
orchardist_petta: To the Song-Steps, when Ives calls, to hear the end? Thirty years of itch, and you've done it in a season. Yes. Let me find a clean apron; I am not standing in ring in this one. Tell Ives yes, and tell Ives I'm bringing my verse.
elder_hazel: Sixty years waiting to know when I'd sing my verse to the one child. It's now, then: a full ring on the Song-Steps, and the last verse after mine. Tell Ives I'm coming. Help me up.
old_tammon: The wheel can turn without me for one evening; it will manage. Tell Ives the Tammon verse will be in its place on the Song-Steps. I'll walk it slow; you walk ahead.
widow_crake: Down off my ridge for a song. My mother would laugh, and then she'd come. Tell Ives yes: the Crake verse comes to the Song-Steps. Go on; I know the way better than you.

hw5.desc: Mother Alder, the oldest chanter living, will sing the counting-song's last verse only to a full ring. For Chanter Ives, invite in person the Speaker at the Grove Ring and Grudge-Keeper Morrow at the Grudge Hall in Heartwood, and Orchardist Petta, Elder Hazel, Old Tammon and the Widow Crake in the Heartwood Fields, then return to Ives on the Song-Steps.
offer: The Speaker sent you. Finish the song. Three words I've waited my whole life on these steps to hear, and now I have to arrange them. Stand up straight; this will be a long day. Here is what finishing the song means.

The last verse of the counting-song belongs to Mother Alder. She is the oldest chanter living, she taught me, she has buried two Speakers, and she has refused to sing that verse for sixty years, on the grounds that, and I quote, you're none of you ready and also my tea is getting cold. She has it. No one else alive does.

And she will sing it to a full ring or not at all. That is the law of the last verse: the ring of families gathered in person, every family that holds a verse and every family that doesn't, to hear the end together, so that no one family carries it alone the way they've carried the pieces. So before anyone sings a note, the ring has to be filled.

That is your errand, and it must be done face to face. Invite each of these in person, and bring me their answer. In the city: the Speaker of the Ring, under the elders at the Grove Ring; and Grudge-Keeper Morrow, at the Grudge Hall.

Out in the Heartwood Fields: Orchardist Petta, in the wild orchards; Elder Hazel, at her orchard gate; Old Tammon, by the brook beside the mill; and the Widow Crake, on the ridge path. Six people in all. Tell each one the same thing: Ives calls a full ring on the Song-Steps, to hear the last verse.

Why you, and not a runner with a bag of notes: a summons to the ring needs a witness, not a courier. You heard the verses given, you walked the trees. By our law the voice that gathered the song is the one that makes the summons official. When you have the six answers, come back to me here on the Song-Steps and I'll call the gathering.
progress: Six invitations, given in person: the Speaker at the Grove Ring and Morrow at the Grudge Hall, here in Heartwood; Petta in the wild orchards, Hazel at her orchard gate, Tammon by the mill brook and the Widow Crake on the ridge path, all in the Heartwood Fields. Then back to me on the Song-Steps.
complete: Six yeses, and look what they've made. The ring is full on the Song-Steps: every family that holds a verse and every family that doesn't. It took an hour, because Heartwood does nothing quickly except grieve. The Tallow family is standing in ring for the first time since the flood year. And there at the back, lawfully, with ink, is Morrow, who strictly wasn't invited. Hush now. Mother Alder is standing up.

Mother Alder: So. A full ring at last, and half of you here out of dread. Good. Before I sing, understand why the end of this song was banned, because you've all been told it wrong. Not because the ending is terrible. Because the ending is a promise, and a promise you can't hurry will eat a city alive if you let it sit on the table. So we put it away, one verse to a family, until the counting was nearly done. The trees say it is.

Mother Alder: Now the verses, one family at a time, each sung by the voice that holds it: Petta, Hazel, Tammon, Crake, the Tallows, all of you. ...And last, the verse we saved for snow, the one I was given to hold: when every elder's branches show, set out the bowls, unbar the door, the morning they come home once more.
Mother Alder: There. The morning they come home once more. That is the end of the counting-song, and that is what this city has been counting toward. Sixty years I carried it. Somebody fetch my tea.

So that's the ending. Not a lament: an instruction. Set the table and open the door, because they are coming home, and the elders flowering means that morning is close. Go to the Speaker at the Grove Ring. The ring has heard its song and must decide what Heartwood does with it, and I think the Speaker has already decided it involves you.

hw6.name: The Speaker's Letter

objective.label: Go west through the Heartwood Fields and along the North Road to Auntie Wren at the Halfway Inn

hw6.desc: The Speaker of the Ring names you Heartwood's envoy. Carry the counting-song, the writ of compensation and the tally of the elders west through the Heartwood Fields and up the North Road to Auntie Wren's Halfway Inn, where Caerdun's envoy already waits and Moonmere's will follow. Grudge-Keeper Morrow meets you at the long table.
offer: Sit, child; the ring has decided, and the trees should hear it said. Here is what Heartwood knows this morning that it did not know in the spring. Four trees of imperial stock, planted the night the empire vanished three hundred years ago, are flowering together, and our own counting-song, finished at last, says what to do when they flower: set out the bowls, unbar the door, the morning they come home once more. The trees and the song agree. They return, and near enough when.

Here is what we don't know. Why they left. Where they went. What returning means for a city built beside the groves they took, holding a writ for every acre. And Heartwood cannot answer that alone, because for three centuries this city has been proudly incurious about its neighbours. Pride is a fine timber. You can't eat it.

The other two cities kept something too; the Speakers before me knew that much and never asked. Caerdun, the garrison the empire locked outside on the Night, has kept a book of what it is owed for three hundred years, and its envoy is already riding for the halfway inn on the North Road, between our two cities. Moonmere, the academy on its island, will come late and pretend it was fashionable. Three cities, three pieces, one table.

You will carry Heartwood's piece: the counting-song, whole, as Mother Alder sang it; the writ of compensation with its 'Restitution upon Return'; and the tally of the ring's flowering, in your own hand. It must be you and not a herald. You gathered the verses, you walked the trees, and by our law the song half belongs to the voice that assembled it. From today the ring names you its Voice.

Morrow: I'm coming too, Speaker, and don't argue; the hall has already minuted it. If the empire is truly walking back through that door, someone must be standing in the doorway holding the bill. Itemised. With interest. Congratulations, explorer: you're the someone. I'll carry the appendices, and I'll meet you at the inn's long table. Don't look pleased, it's unnerving.

The road. Go west out of the West Gate through the Heartwood Fields to the Fields' north-west corner, where the North Road begins. Take the North Road and stay on it through the snow until you reach the halfway inn. Inside, ask Auntie Wren, who keeps it, for the long table, and tell her you are Heartwood's. Take this blade for the road; the pass has spiders.
progress: West out of Heartwood through the Heartwood Fields to the North Road at the Fields' north-west corner, then the North Road through the snow until the halfway inn. Ask Auntie Wren for the long table and say you're Heartwood's. Morrow meets you there.
complete: Heartwood! I'd know that disapproving walk anywhere. Stamp your boots, love, the snow comes in with you or it doesn't come in at all. I'm Wren, this is my inn, and you're the second envoy through that door tonight. In you come; the fire's not offended you yet.

The long table's yours, by the window. Your Morrow's already at it, with a seal the size of a dinner plate and a face like a ledger. The Caerdun one, Duelist-Master Sabel, has been rearranging my salt cellars into columns for an hour. And we're waiting on Moonmere, who are always last and always surprised about it. Sit. Eat. Whatever it is, it'll keep until you've eaten; things usually do.

When the third one's through the door, I'll tell you how my table works and you can all compare your stories. You're not the only one who's come with a story tonight, love, and I've a feeling it's the same one told three ways. I think you'll all get along or die trying.

mm1.name: Shelving

objective.label: Shelve the returns at the Returns Desk, the Moon Stack on the upper shelf and the Two-Moon Stack on the lower, then search the Ferry Crates at the Causeway Landing for a three-moon slip

mm1.desc: Archivist Junn at the Returns Desk is buried in returned books and wants them shelved: one-moon returns on the upper shelf, two-moon returns on the lower, and anything marked with three moons, from the ferry crates at the Causeway Landing, brought to her quietly. The academy has no three-moon collection, and yet the slips keep coming.
offer: Oh good, hands. I'm Junn, Archivist Junn if the Provost is listening, and this is the Returns Desk: every book anyone borrows from the academy's library comes back through here, and I am the one who puts it away. You've come up the causeway into Moonmere, the imperial academy on its island, the last people on Ardenfell who can still read the empire's records. We are very learned and we are drowning in returns.

This week someone borrowed the entire poetry of the second century and gave it back damp. Every volume. Which is either scholarship or a crime, and cataloguing cannot decide, so it has fallen to me, and I have two hands.

Here is how the shelving works. Every returned book carries a slip with a moon mark on it, which says where it lives. One moon: the Moon Stack, the upper shelf, right here beside the desk. Two moons: the Two-Moon Stack, the lower shelf below it. Shelve both stacks for me, the damp ones facing the window so they dry.

Then go down the cloister stair to the Causeway Landing at the bottom of the causeway road, where the ferry has left its crates. Go through them. If you find any slip marked with three moons, do not shelve it anywhere. Bring it to me, and bring it quietly. Because the academy does not have a three-moon collection. And yet the slips keep arriving.

Between us? I love this place, but the catalogue lies. The master index, the great book that lists every shelf in the academy, has an entry for a shelf called row nine hundred, annex. I have looked for it since I first sat at this desk. I have never found it. It is not lost: the index keeps updating that entry, a new book filed to it every few months. Someone is dusting a shelf that isn't there.
Do that, and I'll see you have a pair of proper boots for the stairs. Two stacks on the shelves here, one moon up and two moons down, then the crates at the landing.
progress: The Moon Stack goes to the upper shelf beside my desk, the Two-Moon Stack to the lower shelf, and then the ferry crates down at the Causeway Landing. Anything marked with three moons, bring to me, quietly.
complete: All shelved, nothing further damp, and... you found one. A slip marked with three moons, in the top crate, and look where it says the book belongs: row nine hundred, annex. The shelf I have never found. The catalogue lists it, the ferry delivers to it, and nobody in this academy will admit it exists. See? And yet.

Don't show this slip to anyone. Especially don't show the Provost. Provost Selk runs the academy and Moonmere's court with it, and she keeps the Observatory, the tower on the west side of Academy Court; if a shelf is being hidden on this island, it is being hidden by her office, and I would rather she did not know we were looking. Especially especially don't show the Provost.

Now, the other half of this. Warden Liss keeps the Mending College, the academy's college of healing, across Academy Court on the east side. The night the empire vanished, her college treated the people who reached the shore, and she keeps the infirmary logs from that night. Go to her, tell her I sent you, and ask her what the logs say. She has been wanting a stranger to ask.

mm2.name: The Night of No Sound

objective.label: Cross the causeway to the Moonmere Shores and hear the accounts of the Night from Mereth at the Ferry Piers, Cutter Bram at the Reed Harvest and Lamp-Keeper Orla at the Point

ferry_granddaughter: You're the one Warden Liss sent. I'm Mereth; my grandmother rowed the ferry across the Mere, and she was on the water the night the empire vanished: the last crossing of the evening, an empty boat, coming home to this shore. Liss says the new ones get the whole thing, so here it is, the way she told it every winter of my childhood.

She said the far shore had its evening sounds as she pulled away from it: a dog, a smith working late, cart wheels on the border road. Ordinary as bread. One pull on the oars, two... and between the second pull and the third, the far shore went quiet. Not hushed. Finished. She always said that was the whole story, if you were listening: hushed is a held breath, and you wait for it to let go. Finished is a door, and it has closed.

She rowed back toward it anyway. She beached below a farmhouse with every lamp still lit and bread still warm on the sill, and nobody. The quiet stood in the doorway like it lived there now. She went in and put out the lamps, so the house wouldn't burn. Then she rowed home, and she never crossed at night again for the rest of her life.
cutter_bram: Bread. Liss taught you that. Sit, then, and I'll tell it. My people were out in these beds the night the empire vanished, cutting reed late by lamplight for the college's paper. Across the water the far shore had a smith working, and cart wheels on the road, and then, between one stroke of the blade and the next, it had nothing. Not a shout. Not a cry. The frogs in the beds kept going; the frogs didn't know.

My great-grandfather said the reeds stood straighter afterward, every stem, as if the wind had been told to stop and had obeyed. That is what he said, and that is how we have told it in this family ever since, without adding a word. You've had it the same way.
lamp_keeper_orla: I'm Orla, and I keep the lamp on the Point. It was my family's light before the academy took it over, and we kept it anyway. The night the empire vanished, my grandmother's grandmother was up here trimming the wick. From this arm you can see the border road along the far shore, and that night it was lit end to end with lanterns. She watched them go out. Not blown out one by one, as a wind does it. Finished, all at once, like a page turned.

She kept the lamp lit till dawn in case anyone out on the water rowed toward it. Nobody did. Then she wrote the night down in the lamp book, the way we write every night, and the entry stops mid-word. Nobody in my family has ever finished the sentence. We leave the page as it is.

mm2.desc: Warden Liss of the Mending College wants a newcomer to cross the causeway to the Moonmere Shores and hear, from three families, what they saw and heard on the night the empire vanished: Mereth at the Ferry Piers, Cutter Bram at the Reed Harvest, and Lamp-Keeper Orla at the Point. Then report back to Liss.
offer: Junn sent you. That child will get us all reshelved into a marsh someday. Well. I am Warden Liss, and I keep the Mending College: the academy's college of healing, and the infirmary logs that go back to the night itself. If you are going to dig, dig properly, and start with what my college keeps.

The night the empire vanished, three hundred years ago this year, this college treated the ones who reached the shore by dawn. Farmers from across the water. A ferryman. Two children. No wounds to speak of, not a scratch among them. What they needed mending was elsewhere.

Every account in my log says the same strange thing about that night, and I want you to hear it from the families themselves, not from me. To us, the shore families recite: they have told it to the college so often the words have worn smooth. To a stranger they have to actually remember, and remembering shakes loose what the recitation polished away. You are the stranger. It is the one job in this city only a newcomer can do.

Cross the causeway to the Moonmere Shores and call on three households. Mereth, the Ferryman's Granddaughter, at the Ferry Piers, west along the shore from the causeway head; her grandmother was on the water that night. Cutter Bram at the Reed Harvest, the east beds; take a loaf of bread with you, it opens that door faster than my name does. And Lamp-Keeper Orla at the Point, the lamp out on the west arm; her family has kept the lamp book since before the academy took the lamp over.
Hear each story to the end. Do not hurry them and do not finish their sentences. Then come back and tell me what you heard, and I will tell you what it means.
progress: Three households on the Moonmere Shores, across the causeway: Mereth at the Ferry Piers, Cutter Bram at the Reed Harvest in the east beds, with bread, and Lamp-Keeper Orla at the Point on the west arm. Hear each account to the end, then come back to me.
complete: You heard it, then. Three families who were awake that night, on the water, in the reeds, at the lamp, and not one of them heard a thing. Not screaming. Not thunder. Not a bell. The far shore simply stopped. A whole empire gone between one wave and the next, and the loudest thing on the Mere that night was the water on the causeway stones.

That is what my log says, in every hand, from every patient we treated: no sound. I have had thirty years to think about what it means, and it comes to this. Things that end violently are loud. A city falling makes a noise. Things that leave on schedule are quiet. Nobody shouts when they are leaving at the time they meant to.

Now you know what the Mending College has known for three centuries and never once said at dinner. The next thread is not mine to pull. Master Corvo teaches fire at the Burned Shelf, the academy's other college, across Academy Court on the west side, beside the Observatory. Ask him why his college is called that. He has been waiting a long time for someone to ask who was not a member.

mm3.name: The Burned Shelf

objective.label: Wade the strand below the causeway landing and bring back 4 drowned book spines

mm3.desc: Master Corvo of the Burned Shelf says the academy burned its own astronomy books the week after the empire vanished, and forbids its members from going near the site. The Mere took some of the burning books first. Wade the strand below the Causeway Landing, east of the causeway, and bring Corvo 4 Burned Book Spines.
offer: So you're the one pulling threads. Liss sent you to ask about the name, and I am going to tell you, because I have been waiting twenty years for somebody who was not a member of this college to ask. I am Master Corvo. I teach fire at the Burned Shelf, and my college takes its name from a fire.

The week after the vanishing, when the academy had just watched the whole far shore go dark, it burned its own astronomy section. Every book, every table, every chart of the sky. Deliberately. Indoors. Not a mob, not an accident: the masters of this academy carried the books into one room and set them alight, and now we teach fire magic in that room. The Provost calls that economy. I call it a confession with seating.

But burned books drown badly. The room stands over the water, and the Mere took some of the books before the fire finished with them; and the Mere, unlike this institution, keeps everything. Its current runs north round the island and lays what it takes on the spit below the causeway.

Here is why it must be you. Every member of this college is forbidden, by standing order of the Provost's office, from disturbing the site of the founding fire or anything the sea took from it. A remarkably specific rule for a place that claims to remember nothing. You are not a member. The rule slides right off you. Also, my students float.

So: wade the strand below the Causeway Landing, on the east side of the causeway, and work the sea bed. The spines of the drowned books lie among the stones, three hundred years tanned by salt. Bring me four Burned Book Spines; anything with letters still on it. I don't care how ruined. There is a willow staff on this bench for whoever does it, and I have never once offered a student anything.
progress: The strand below the Causeway Landing, east of the causeway: wade in and work the sea bed. Four Burned Book Spines, anything with letters left on it, back to my bench at the Burned Shelf.
complete: Give them here. Look at the titles, what the salt left of them. Tables of Conjunction. Ephemeris, Years One Through... the number's burned off, of course it is. An ephemeris is a table of where the stars and the moons will stand on every night for years to come. These are date tables. All four of them. The academy burned its date tables.

Think what that means. You don't burn what you fear; that's superstition, and this academy has never been superstitious a day in its life. You burn what you've finished. They computed something, the week after the shore went dark. They wrote the answer down fair. And then they burned every table anyone could have used to check their work.

Ask yourself what kind of answer deserves that. I have asked for twenty years, and the Provost has never once answered me, which is an answer of a kind. She will have heard about you by now; nothing is waded for on this island without her knowing. When she sends for you, go to her at the Observatory, the tower on the west side of Academy Court, and do whatever she gives you to do. Watch what she does not say.

mm4.name: The Provost's Kindness

objective.label: Stamp the winter permits: registry, bursar, then the harbourmaster's stamp across the causeway

mm4.desc: Provost Selk has set you to stamping the winter permit renewals: the registry's stamp first, then the bursar's, then the harbourmaster's across the causeway at the Causeway Head, and the finished box back to her desk at the Observatory. It feels very much like make-work.
offer: Ah. The new archivist's assistant. I am Provost Selk; I am head of this academy and of Moonmere's court, and I keep the Observatory, which is where you are standing. I hear excellent things of you, which always worries me; excellence is so rarely convenient.
I am told you have been wading. The strand is cold at this season and the college is grateful for the exercise, I'm sure. I have work better suited to your talents, and a good deal drier.

This box holds the winter permit renewals: the academy's leave for every ferryman, reed-seller and student to cross the causeway and land on this island through the storm months. Each form must be stamped by three offices, and it must be stamped in order.

First the Registry Stamp, at the registry's desk down in the academy court between this tower and the Returns Desk. Second the Bursar's Stamp, in the Bursar's Office a little further along the same side of the court. Third the Harbourmaster's Stamp, which is across the causeway at the Causeway Head on the Shores, beside the fares board.

Registry, bursar, harbourmaster. Not bursar first because the registry was busy; not harbourmaster first because you happened to be on the Shores. The order matters. The order has always mattered, for reasons that were once reasons.

When the third stamp is down, bring the finished box back across the causeway to my desk here. There is a woldcloth robe in it for you, which is more than the bursar has had out of me in a decade. Off you go.
progress: The winter permits, every form, in order: the Registry Stamp in the academy court, then the Bursar's Stamp beside it, then across the causeway to the Harbourmaster's Stamp at the Causeway Head. Then the box back to my desk at the Observatory. Yes, this is the task.
complete: Finished? Remarkable. Most give up at the second stamp, and the ones who don't usually transfer to Caerdun, where the tedium is at least armed. Put the box there. Here is your robe, and here is something you did not ask for.

Do you know what an archive is for? Not remembering; any attic remembers. An archive is for deciding when. When a thing is safe to know. When it stops being a knife and becomes a key. My predecessors decided a certain when about a certain thing, and I have spent my whole tenure hoping it would not fall to me. You may go.

Archivist Junn, later, at your elbow: Psst. Permit season ended a month ago. Nobody renews a winter permit in this month; she invented a mountain of stamps to keep you in a chair for a day. Which means you frightened her, which means we're close.

Archivist Junn: And I found it. The annex key exists. The academy keeps a registry of keys, every door and who has borrowed it, and under row nine hundred, annex, the borrower column has said the same thing for three hundred years: the Provost's office. She is not hiding a room from us. She is keeping it. Come and find me at the Returns Desk. I have a plan, and I need you for it.

mm5.name: The Telescope Room

objective.label: Meet Junn at the observatory after the last bell and open the annex door behind the star-globe

mm5.desc: Junn means to open the hidden annex tonight. Meet her on the Observatory stair after the last bell and open the Annex Door behind the star-globe, the door the Provost's office has held the key to for three hundred years.
offer: Tonight. Meet me on the observatory stair after the last bell, the one that closes the library for the night. The cloisters empty in a quarter of an hour after it, the Provost goes up to her office at the top of the tower, and nobody uses that stair till morning.

Look at what we have. A slip that files a book to a shelf no one can find. Three families who heard the far shore go quiet, not loud. Four burned date tables the academy would rather we had left on the sea bed. And a key to row nine hundred, annex, borrowed by the Provost's office for three hundred years running. Every thread runs into the Observatory. I don't think the shelf is a shelf. I think it is a room.

The Annex Door is behind the star-globe on the observatory stair: the great brass globe of the heavens on its landing, halfway up. Behind it there is a door with no shelf-mark and no number, and somebody has dusted it. I have checked the masonry around it twice, in daylight, pretending to admire the globe. It is a real door and it is not bricked up.
And I've brought a pry-bar. It is the most illegal thing I have ever held, so please look impressed.

I'll say this once and then I'll be brave. I'm frightened. Not of the Provost: of being right. If the academy has kept a room shut for three hundred years and kept it dusted, then whatever is in it was worth three hundred years of lying to every person on this island, and I would like to know what that is before I decide how angry to be.
So: the Observatory, the tower on the west side of Academy Court. Climb the stair to the star-globe after the last bell. Open the Annex Door. We're going in.
progress: The Observatory, after the last bell, when the cloisters are empty. Climb the stair to the star-globe on its landing, and open the Annex Door behind it. I'll be there with the pry-bar.
complete: Provost Selk, from the stair: Before you scratch my window frames, archivist: the key turns clockwise. Don't gape, Junn, it ages you. I have known where the two of you were going since the stamps. If this door must open, then it opens properly, with its keeper present and the key in the lock. That was always the rule. That was the whole rule.

Provost Selk: Come in, then, and look. This is the annex, row nine hundred: the shelf that is a room. Every telescope here was found exactly as you see it the morning after the vanishing, every one trained on the same empty point of sky. The water-clock has run since that night; my office winds it. The log on the desk is the astronomers' record. Read its final line aloud, Junn. It is time it was said in a voice.

Archivist Junn: ...Coordinates. A point in the sky, the point they are all aimed at. And a date. Provost, that date is close. Not a hundred years off: close. You knew. The academy has always known the day.

Provost Selk: Yes. The morning after the Night, the astronomers computed something, wrote this one line, burned every table that could check it, and sealed the room. Because a date you cannot hasten is not knowledge, Junn, it is a sentence, and my predecessors decided this island was kinder not knowing the day it was waiting for. They called the concealment mercy. For most of my life I agreed with them. Note the tense.

Provost Selk: Forty years I have wound that clock alone. You two are the first people to stand in this room with me, and I find I mind that less than I expected to. Sleep, both of you. Then come to me here at the Observatory in the morning: there is something the academy must now do, and I would rather do it with you in the room.

mm6.name: Mercy, Rescinded

objective.label: With Junn, cross the Moonmere Shores, take the Shore Road to the Heartwood Fields and the North Road beyond, and ask Auntie Wren at the Halfway Inn for the long table

mm6.desc: Provost Selk has ended the academy's three-hundred-year silence. Carry the sealed observation log, with Junn, to Auntie Wren's Halfway Inn on the North Road, where Caerdun's and Heartwood's envoys are already waiting, and tell them everything, beginning with the apology.
offer: You came. Good. Sit. This is the part my predecessors never had to say. For three hundred years this academy has known the day written in that log and told no one on this island, and we called that mercy. I want you to understand why, before I tell you it is over.

The mathematics of mercy have inverted. When the date was far off, telling people was cruelty: you would hand a fisherman's family a morning their great-grandchildren might see and ask them to live every day under it. But the date is close now, and the sum runs the other way. Not telling them means that people meet that morning unwarned, in their nightclothes, with the door unbarred. Concealment has become the cruelty. So: we end it. The mercy is rescinded, by the Provost, today.

Here is what the line in the log says, plainly, since plainness is new to us. A point of sky, the one every telescope upstairs is still aimed at, and a morning. The astronomers who wrote it believed that on that morning the empire comes back to the land it left, and they did not trust this island to live with knowing which morning. Whether they were right, Moonmere must not decide alone.

Caerdun's envoy and Heartwood's are already at the halfway inn: Auntie Wren's inn on the North Road, halfway between those two cities and on neither one's ground. We watch the roads; we're secretive, not blind.

You and Junn will carry the sealed log. All of it: the coordinates, the date, the fire, and the shame. The finder carries; that is the academy's oldest rule, and you two found it: Junn found the thread, and you refused to drop it. The academy will enter you in its book as the Finder of the Annex.

The road. Cross the causeway to the Moonmere Shores, and take the Shore Road out of them to the north-east. It runs the warm coast to the Heartwood Fields; cross the Fields to the North Road at their north-west corner, and stay on the road through the snow until you reach the inn. Ask Auntie Wren for the long table and tell her you are Moonmere's.
One instruction, and it is not optional. When you stand before the other two cities and open this log, tell them everything. And begin with the apology.
progress: Cross the causeway to the Shores, take the Shore Road north-east to the Heartwood Fields, then the North Road to the halfway inn; Junn goes with you. Ask Auntie Wren for the long table, say you are Moonmere's, and begin with the apology.
complete: And here's Moonmere, last as always, with snow on your fancy collars. Stamp your boots, loves, the snow comes in with you or it doesn't come in at all. I'm Wren; Auntie Wren to everyone who has ever eaten here, and that's everyone. This is the Halfway Inn, and the long table is the one by the fire. In, in.

The other two are already at it. Caerdun's envoy, Duelist-Master Sabel, has been sorting my salt cellars into ledger columns for an hour, and Heartwood's, Grudge-Keeper Morrow, has been correcting her sums. They're mid-argument about whether a promise counts as a debt, and I've not followed a word of it, but I've kept an inn forty years and I know a table that's been waiting for its third chair.

You're just in time to make it worse. Sit. Eat. Whatever it is you've carried up that road, it'll keep until you've eaten; things usually do. Stew's on, and when the bowls are empty I'll call that table to order myself, and the three envoys can say their pieces in turn while you listen. Nobody keeps anything back, not at my table.

inn1.name: What Three Cities Knew

objective.label: Hear all three testimonies at the long table: Sabel's, Morrow's and Junn's

duelist_sabel: Sabel, of Caerdun. Caerdun brings arithmetic. Our paymaster's vault turned up an imperial wage schedule, genuine down to the ink: it pays our garrison its wages in advance, year on year, for three hundred years, and it ends in a single settlement of every debt owed us, in full, on one date. The date is near. The sealed imperial clock in the tower beside our court counts to the same day.

Think about what that means. The empire doesn't just live; it budgets. You don't budget for a day you won't see. Whoever wrote that schedule intended to be standing in Caerdun on the morning it falls due, with the money.
grudgekeeper_morrow: Morrow, of Heartwood; I keep the grudge hall, the floor that records everything the empire took from us. Heartwood brings the word Caerdun's ledgers were too polite to write: Return. Capital letter. It's in the writ of compensation they left for our felled groves, 'Restitution upon Return', and it's in the counting-song they left in our mouths, one verse a year since the night they vanished.

And the four mourning trees they planted at our ring the night they left are imperial stock, bred to flower once, all together, at full growth. They are flowering now, on schedule, to mark the song's last verse. They didn't just plan to come back. They wanted us counting.
archivist_junn: Junn, of Moonmere. Moonmere brings... first, an apology. We knew the date. The academy has known the date since the morning after the vanishing, when every telescope in our observatory was found aimed at the same empty point in the sky. Within the week the Provosts had sealed the room. They called the concealment mercy. I'm not old enough to defend that and I'm not going to try.

Here is the sealed log from that room. Its final entry is a set of coordinates and a day. The same day as Caerdun's settlement. The same day as Heartwood's last verse. We never compared, so none of us knew we were all holding the same page.

inn1.desc: At the Halfway Inn on the North Road, Auntie Wren has seated the three cities' envoys at one table: Duelist-Master Sabel for Caerdun, Grudge-Keeper Morrow for Heartwood and Archivist Junn for Moonmere. Hear each one's testimony in turn, Sabel first, then Morrow, then Junn, and come back to Wren.
offer: Sit down, love, before you fall down; you've walked half the North Road in snow. This is the Halfway Inn, I'm Wren, and this is my long table. It sits on neither city's ground, which is the whole point of it, and tonight it's holding three cities' worth of secrets, so it gets house rules.
House rules for history being made: bowls stay full, voices stay down, and nobody stabs the table. It's older than all your grievances put together and I'd like to keep it that way.

Here's what you've walked into. Three envoys came to my inn on one night, one from each city, each sent by their court with a piece of the same old story, and each, I'd wager, under orders to keep it close until they'd heard the others. Caerdun's piece is about money. Heartwood's is about a promise. Moonmere's is about a date, and they've sat on it a long while. Nobody has put the three together yet, and that's what tonight is for.

So: go round the table and hear all three, and in this order, because they've argued about it already. Caerdun first, that's Duelist-Master Sabel, the one who's been arranging my salt cellars into ledger columns for an hour. Then Heartwood's envoy, Grudge-Keeper Morrow, the tall one with the disapproving walk, who keeps her city's record of everything the empire took. Then Moonmere, Archivist Junn, the young one with the sealed book, who was sent here with orders to begin with an apology.

Hear them to the end. Don't interrupt Sabel, don't argue with Morrow, and don't let Junn apologise twice. When all three have had their say, come back to me and I'll tell you what you've just heard, because somebody at this table ought to say it plainly.
progress: Round the table, love, in order: Sabel for Caerdun, then Morrow for Heartwood, then Junn for Moonmere, and hear each one to the end. Then back to me. The stew will keep; stew always does.
complete: So. Let me say it the way it sounds from behind a counter. Caerdun has a payment date. Heartwood has a promise to return, and trees that say when. Moonmere has the day itself, written down the morning after. Three pieces of one page, and the three of you held one each for three hundred years like a family that can't discuss anything at supper.
Sabel: Then let one of us say it out loud, so it's been said. They left on purpose. They meant to come back. And they're nearly due.
Morrow: Well. I've waited my whole life to be this angry, and now that it's here I find I mostly want to sit down. Wren, whatever's strongest that isn't the stew.

Sit down, all of you, you've earned it. Junn's not finished with that log of hers, I can see it in her face, so when you've eaten, go and ask her what else is in it. She's got one more line to read you, and it's about the gates.

inn2.name: Letters of Passage

objective.label: Carry the letters of passage to any one of the three courts' rulers

inn2.desc: The academy's log shows the locks on the three Border Gates are timed to open ahead of the date. The courts have signed letters of passage so every court's charter is honoured at every gate. Carry the letters to any one of the three rulers: the Lord Marshal in Caerdun's Parade Square, the Speaker of the Ring at Heartwood's Grove Ring, or Provost Selk in Moonmere's Observatory.
offer: There's one more line in the log I haven't read you, and it's the urgent one. The annex in our observatory didn't only hold the telescopes; it held the empire's border survey, the plans of the wall and the three Border Gates. And by those plans, the locks on the gates aren't broken. They were never broken. They're timed: set, three hundred years ago, to open ahead of the date.

Which is why all three gates unlocked themselves on the same morning this spring, and why our courts' wardens have been holding the leaves shut with their shoulders ever since. You air a house out before the family gets home. Somebody wrote that down as an instruction.

Sabel: Then the courts stop being rivals for a morning and start being neighbours with one very large shared wall. Letters of passage, three copies: each court honours a charter from either of the other two at every Border Gate, so any explorer with any court's paper may go in. The rulers agreed by rider overnight; it only wants the seals. Sign here, here, and... Morrow, your seal is the size of a dinner plate, how do you carry it.
Morrow: With conviction.

And one more thing, and it's for you specifically. The courts need a sworn witness of record: someone who sat at this table and heard all three testimonies, and can stand at a Border Gate and say what this is and isn't. Your court named you before we'd finished asking.

So, the job.
