Take these three letters and put them in any one ruler's hands, whichever is nearest or dearest: the Lord Marshal, who keeps to the Parade Square in Caerdun; the Speaker of the Ring, under the four elders at Heartwood's Grove Ring; or Provost Selk, in the Observatory in Moonmere. One ruler is enough; the courts exchange the countersigned copies between themselves, and your own court will welcome the familiar face. Then go to any Border Gate, hear its warden's account of the opening, and remember everything. You're the record now.
progress: The three letters of passage to any one ruler: the Lord Marshal in Caerdun's Parade Square, the Speaker of the Ring at Heartwood's Grove Ring, or Provost Selk in Moonmere's Observatory. Then make for a Border Gate and hear its warden.
complete: Received, read, and countersigned. These letters go out to the other two courts by rider tonight, and from first light every Border Gate admits every explorer, whichever court's charter they carry. The gate wardens have their orders: at first light they stand back and let the leaves swing, and nobody holds them shut again.

You understand what you've put your name under, witness. For three hundred years nobody went through those gates, by treaty and by fear. Tomorrow people will. Whatever is on the other side has waited a long time to be seen, and a court will believe what you saw before it believes what it was told. Go to any Border Gate, hear its warden, and then go through.

Each court keeps a scout at a forward camp past its gate: Scout Bettany at the Hunting Lodge in the Hunting Wood, past Caerdun's gate; Scout Wenna at Plantation Cross in the Timber Estates, past Heartwood's; Scout Ilva up the road from the gate in the Summer Lakes, past Moonmere's. Report to the scout past the gate you take.

The gate warden, later, at the Border Gate: Three hundred years my family has watched this door. My mother told me you could put your ear to it on a cold night and hear ticking, and we all said it was the wind being cruel. It wasn't the wind. It was never the wind. The courts' letter says I stand back at first light, so I stand back. Stand back yourself, envoy. It's opening.
The gate warden: The scout's camp is just past the gate. Report there first; the scout will tell you what's in there before you learn it the hard way.

ds1_cd.name: The Held Breath

objective.label: Chart the Hunting Wood for the court's map: reach the Hunting Lodge, the King's Rides and the Swallowed Garrison

ds1_cd.desc: Scout Bettany at Caerdun's Forward Camp needs the Hunting Wood charted before the court's supply trains come through the gate. Reach the three marked places, the Hunting Lodge, the King's Rides and the Swallowed Garrison, then report back to the camp. Avoid fighting the empire's sentinels if you can; they mostly just ask you to leave.
offer: You found the camp. Good; the polite one at the gate tells everybody the household isn't receiving, and some of them turn round. I'm Bettany, Caerdun's scout; the court sent me through ahead of you to find out what's in here, and this camp beside the Hunting Lodge is as far as I've got. Whatever you were expecting through that gate: wrong. I've been over the threshold twice now and I still dream about it.

It's not a ruin. Ruins are honest; things fall down and stay down. In there, the beds are made. The tables are set. This whole province was the emperors' hunting park, the Hunting Wood: lodges, rides cut straight through the trees so a king could see his stag, and a garrison to guard it all. Three hundred years of wild has grown up through all of it, and underneath the wild, a country holding its breath.

Two warnings. The beasts are beasts; you know beasts, though these are the empire's hunting stock gone feral, and big. The sentinels are the thing to understand. They're the empire's caretakers, still working, still enforcing the law of a country that isn't here. They call the empire's people the household, as if the empire were one great house, and to them we are trespassers on its grounds. Mostly that means they ask you to leave. Politely. Forever. Do not fight one if you can be boring instead.

Here's the job, and why it can't wait. The court is sending settlers' supply trains, mule trains, through this gate within the month, and right now our entire map of the province is the word trees and my bad memory. I need three places charted. First, the Hunting Lodge, the king's lodge this camp sits beside; walk up to it properly and note what state it's in. Second, the King's Rides, the three straight avenues cut through the wood. Third, the Swallowed Garrison, the old garrison post the trees have grown over.

Reach all three, then come back here to the camp and tell me what you saw, and I'll draw it. If a sentinel stops you, be boring. I've been practising. There are two Hi-Potions in the court's stores for you when you're back; charting is slower than it looks, and the beasts don't wait for the ink to dry.
progress: Three places for the map: the Hunting Lodge beside this camp, the King's Rides, the straight avenues through the wood, and the Swallowed Garrison the trees have grown over. Reach all three, then back to me at the camp. Be boring with the sentinels.
complete: A sentinel, on the road: Good morning. You are trespassing on household grounds. Before your company came, the register of trespass held four hundred and eleven notices, all to one resident. Yours are entered beneath them. Compliance to date: zero. I am instructed to add, in cases of repeated offence: please.
See? Politely. Forever. Four hundred and eleven notices, and every one of them to the same person; I'd give a week's pay to know who, and so would the court. But that isn't our job today.

This is a good chart. Lodge, rides, garrison; the court's mules can come through on this. Here are your Hi-Potions, and here's the next thing, which I'll tell you now so you can sleep on it. There's a place at the heart of this province the maps mark like it matters: the Mausoleum, the tomb of the emperors, under the ridge to the north-west. Every paper we've found in here points at it. That's tomorrow's problem, and tomorrow's problem is always yours. Come and see me when you've rested.

ds2_cd.name: Your Trial

objective.label: Enter by the Mausoleum Door, fight through the Mausoleum to the Emperors' Vault at its heart, and break the seal on the Sealed Notice

ds2_cd.desc: Every record in the Hunting Wood says its founding terms are kept at the Mausoleum. Scout Bettany wants the province's founding writ, the empire's own statement of what the land is and who may hold it. Enter by the Mausoleum Door, north-west under the ridge, fight through to the Emperors' Vault and break the seal on the Sealed Notice.
offer: Rested? Good. Now the part the court actually sent us for. Every record we've pulled in this province, every ledger in the lodge and every order nailed to a tree, ends the same way: original terms retained at... and then it names the deep place. The Mausoleum. The tomb of the emperors of Vanai, dug under the ridge to the north-west of here.

What's kept there is the province's founding writ: the empire's own statement, in its own words, of what this land is and who may hold it. Every province was given one when the empire laid it out. Ours is lodged at the heart of the Mausoleum, under seal, and nothing has disturbed it in three hundred years.

Why it matters. The three courts are about to spend a generation arguing over who has custody of these provinces now that the gates are open, and whoever holds the original wording holds the argument. More than that: the sentinels take their standing orders from that writ. Every notice of trespass they've issued comes out of whatever it says. Recover it, and we finally know the rules we've been trespassing against.

So: find the Mausoleum Door, north-west under the ridge; it's marked on your chart now. Go down into the Mausoleum. It is kept, like everything in here, and what keeps it will not want you there; fight through whatever still stands guard, hall by hall, to the vault at its heart, the Emperors' Vault. There is a notice under wax on the empty bier there, the Sealed Notice. Break the seal, read it, and bring me its words exactly.
The court has a Greywall Hauberk, garrison pattern, waiting for whoever brings the writ out, and a Remedy, because I've seen the teeth on what's down there. After you.
progress: The Mausoleum Door, north-west under the ridge. Down through the Mausoleum to the Emperors' Vault at its heart, and the Sealed Notice on the empty bier. Break the seal, read the writ, and bring me its exact words.
complete: The Warden of the Mausoleum: Halt. Names, please, for the visitors' list. ...None of you appear. The most recent visitor attended a funeral two hundred and ninety-nine years ago and signed only: sorry. You may proceed as mourners, unscheduled. The emperors are sleeping.

You're out, and you've got it. Read it to me again. The household departs this night and will return. Keep out. Keep well. That's the whole writ? The founding terms of this whole province, lodges, rides and all: one line.

And here's what came down the road from the other forward camps while you were under: it's the same document in every province. Word for word. The household departs this night and will return. Keep out. Keep well. So the empire didn't leave each province its own terms. It left one order, everywhere, the night it went.

Two orders, one breath. Keep out: that's the sentinels' notices, and three hundred years of a shut gate. Keep well: that's the beds made and the tables set. I can't decide if that's a threat or a kindness, and I'm starting to suspect it's both. Your hauberk and your Remedy, and the title the court is sending with them: Witness of the Doorstep.

Every province's papers point one way from here: the Reservoir, the drowned valley south of this wood, down the Reservoir Road. The three courts are raising a joint camp on its shore, and Duelist-Master Sabel of Caerdun is there with the other two envoys. Go to her at the Joint Camp. She'll have work for you the moment you arrive; she always does.

ds1_hw.name: The Held Breath

objective.label: Chart the Timber Estates: reach the Ranks, the Log Flume and the Timber Yards for the court's map

ds1_hw.desc: Scout Wenna at Heartwood's Forward Camp needs the Timber Estates charted before the court's settlers' supply trains come through the gate: reach the Ranks, the Log Flume and the Timber Yards, avoid fighting the sentinels, and come back to the camp at Plantation Cross.
offer: You made it up from the gate. I'm Wenna, Heartwood's scout; the court sent me through at first light, ahead of you, and this camp at Plantation Cross is as far as anyone from our side has got. Whatever you were expecting through that gate: wrong. I've been over the threshold twice now and I still dream about it.

This is the Timber Estates. Heartwood's groves, once, before the empire felled them and replanted the land in ruler-straight rows for its timber; every tree in this province stands where a clerk told it to. It's the first province inside the border, Heartwood's doorstep, and in three hundred years nobody from our side has walked it end to end.

It's not a ruin. Ruins are honest; things fall down and stay down. In there, the beds in the foresters' huts are made. The tables are set. Three hundred years of wild growing up through all of it, and underneath the wild, a country holding its breath.

Two warnings. The beasts are beasts; you know beasts, and there are plenty. But the sentinels, the empire's caretakers, the metal ones, are still working, and they enforce the law of a country that isn't here. They'll call this household grounds: the household is their word for the empire's people, as if the whole country were one great house they're keeping. Mostly that means they ask you to leave. Politely. Forever. Don't fight them if you can be boring instead. I've been practising.

Here's the job and why it can't wait. The court is sending settlers' supply trains through this gate within the month, mule trains with families behind them, and right now our entire map of the province is the word trees and my bad memory.

I need three places charted, all marked on this slate: the Ranks, the great planted rows; the Log Flume, the chute the empire sent its timber down; and the Timber Yards, where the cut logs were stacked. Reach each one, mark the slate, and come back to me here.
progress: Three places in the Timber Estates for the court's map: the Ranks, the Log Flume and the Timber Yards, all marked on your slate. If a sentinel stops you, be boring. Then back to me at the forward camp at Plantation Cross.
complete: A Sentinel, on the road: Good morning. You are trespassing on household grounds. Before your company came, the register of trespass held four hundred and eleven notices, all to one resident. Yours are entered beneath them. Compliance to date: zero. I am instructed to add, in cases of repeated offence: please.

See? Politely. Forever. Four hundred and twelve notices, not one of them ever stopped anybody, and it still says please. Good chart. The Ranks, the Flume, the Yards and the ground between: the court's mule trains can follow this. I'll copy it fair tonight and send it back through the gate.

One more thing while you've got your breath. There's a place at the heart of this province the old maps mark like it matters: the Overseer's Lodge, the house the whole estate was run from, east among the ranks. Every paper I've picked up out here points at it. That's tomorrow's problem, and tomorrow's problem is always yours: when you're ready, talk to me here and I'll tell you what we think is in it. Rest here tonight; ours is the only fire for miles.

ds2_hw.name: Your Trial

objective.label: Enter the Overseer's Lodge by the Overseer's Door east among the ranks, fight through it, and break the seal on the Sealed Notice on the overseer's desk

ds2_hw.desc: Scout Wenna wants the Timber Estates' founding writ, the empire's own statement of what the province is and who may hold it, recovered from the Overseer's Lodge: enter by the Overseer's Door east among the ranks, fight down to the overseer's office, and break the seal on the Sealed Notice on the desk.
offer: Now the part the court actually sent us for. Every record I've pulled in this province, every felling docket and survey sheet, ends the same way: a stamp reading 'original terms retained at', and then the name of one place. The Overseer's Lodge. The house this whole estate was run from, east among the ranks, behind the Overseer's Door.

What's kept there is the province's founding writ. Not a copy. The empire's own statement, under its own seal, of what this land is and who may hold it. For the Timber Estates that means: by what right they felled Heartwood's groves and planted these rows, and on what terms.

Why it matters, in order. First, the courts are about to spend a generation arguing over who holds the interior now that the gates are open, and whoever holds the original wording holds the argument; Heartwood would very much like that to be Heartwood. Second, the sentinels here take their standing orders from that writ. Recover it and we finally know the rules we've been trespassing against, instead of guessing them from a metal clerk's manners.

Here is the trial. Go east through the ranks to the Overseer's Door. Descend into the Overseer's Lodge; the clerks' halls come first, and the overseer's office is at the heart of it. The lodge is still kept, by things that will not be boring back; fight through whatever still holds it. On the overseer's desk you'll find a notice under wax: the Sealed Notice. Break the seal, read it, and bring me its words, exactly.

I'd come with you, but one of us has to be able to report back if the other doesn't. That's you going in, and me standing here feeling badly about it. There's a jerkin in it, thornhide, Heartwood's own, and the court will put a title on you for it. After you.
progress: The Overseer's Lodge, through the Overseer's Door east among the ranks. Fight down to the overseer's office, break the wax on the Sealed Notice on the desk, and bring me its exact words here at the forward camp.
complete: The Overseer's Automaton: Roll call. Shift the first: absent. Shift the second: absent. Shift the third: absent. Three hundred years of perfect attendance, all marked absent, excused, household business. Are you the relief crew? You are not on the rota. Nobody is on the rota. I have kept the rota anyway. One must.

You've got it. Read it to me again, slowly. 'The household departs this night and will return. Keep out. Keep well.' That's all? That's all. Word's just come from the other two forward camps, Caerdun's in the Hunting Wood and Moonmere's in the Summer Lakes: it's the same document in every province, word for word. The household: that's them, the empire's people. Departs this night: they left on purpose, and wrote it down the night they went. Will return. And then two orders.

Keep out. Keep well. Two orders, one breath. Read it one way and it's a threat: stay away from what's ours; it's why the gates stayed locked and why the sentinels write their notices. Read it the other and it's a kindness: look after yourselves while we're gone; it's why the beds are made. Three hundred years and I can't decide which they meant, and I'm starting to suspect it's both. Heartwood holds the original terms now, and you're the witness who carried them out.

And here's where every province's papers point from here. Half the ledgers in that lodge carry one more stamp: 'original retained at the valley archive'. The valley archive is in the Reservoir, the drowned valley deeper in, and the three courts are raising a joint camp on its shore.

The way there is over the Gardens pass, as Heartwood's own people went: take the Gardens Road out of the west side of the Estates into the King's Gardens, cross the Gardens to their far western side, and go down the Gardens Pass into the Reservoir. Duelist-Master Sabel of Caerdun, who sat with you at Wren's table, is already at the Joint Camp on the shore. Go to her and tell her Heartwood's doorstep is read.

ds1_mm.name: The Held Breath

objective.label: Chart the Summer Lakes for the court's map: reach the Great Lake, the Boathouse Crescent and the Ballroom Dome

ds1_mm.desc: Scout Ilva at Moonmere's Forward Camp needs the Summer Lakes charted before the court's supply trains come through the gate: stand at the Great Lake, the Boathouse Crescent and the Ballroom Dome, and come back to the camp. The empire's sentinels still patrol; be boring, not brave.
offer: You made it up the road. I'm Ilva, scout for Moonmere's court, and this is Moonmere's Forward Camp: the court's first toehold inside the border, a few tents up the road from the Border Gate that stood shut three hundred years and swung open for you this morning. Here is the map. It is mostly blank. That is why you are here.

First, whatever you were expecting of the Summer Lakes: wrong. I've been over the threshold twice now and I still dream about it. It isn't a ruin. Ruins are honest; things fall down and stay down. In there, the beds are made. The tables are set. The lawns are cut. This was the empire's resort, villas and boathouses where its great families summered, and three hundred years of wild has grown up through all of it, and underneath the wild there is a country holding its breath.

Two warnings. The beasts are beasts; you know beasts. But the sentinels: the empire's caretakers, the servants it left behind to keep the place, still working, still enforcing the law of a country that isn't here. Don't fight them if you can be boring instead. Mostly they ask you to leave. Politely. Forever. Nod, say nothing interesting, and walk on.

Here's the job, and why it can't wait. The court is sending settlers' supply trains through this gate within the month, mules and carts and people who have never been inside, and right now our entire map of the province is the word lakes and my bad memory. I need the three places that matter charted by someone who has stood in them.

Walk the Summer Lakes edge to edge and reach the three places I've marked on this slate. The Great Lake, straight on up the road from this camp, the big water the whole province is built around. The Boathouse Crescent, round on the east shore, where the household kept its boats. And the Ballroom Dome, away to the north-west on the far side, where a dome stands up out of the west mere. Then come back here to the camp. If a sentinel stops you, be boring. I've been practising.
progress: Three places for the court's map: the Great Lake up the road from the camp, the Boathouse Crescent on the east shore, and the Ballroom Dome to the north-west over the west mere. Stand at each, then come back to me at the forward camp. If a sentinel stops you, be boring.
complete: A Sentinel, on the road: Good morning. You are trespassing on household grounds. Before your company came, the register of trespass held four hundred and eleven notices, all to one resident. Yours are entered beneath them. Compliance to date: zero. I am instructed to add, in cases of repeated offence: please.

Scout Ilva: See? Politely. Forever. Household grounds, it said; that is their word for all this. The household is what the sentinels call the empire's people, the whole country as one great house with the family away, and everything inside the border is the house's grounds. Which makes us something walking on the lawn. Good chart, by the way. The three places are on the slate, and the supply trains will have a map that is more than a word.

Scout Ilva: Now, about that dome. There's a place at the heart of this province the maps mark like it matters: the Sunken Ballroom, under the west mere, below the dome you stood beside. Every record we've pulled from the villas points at it. That's tomorrow's problem, and tomorrow's problem is always yours. Rest, and come and find me here at the camp when you're ready for it.

ds2_mm.name: Your Trial

objective.label: Descend into the sunken ballroom, fight through whatever still keeps it, and break the seal on the writ at its heart

ds2_mm.desc: Every record in the Summer Lakes says the province's founding writ, the empire's own statement of what this land is and who may hold it, lies at the heart of the Sunken Ballroom under the west mere. Go down the Ballroom Stair, fight through to the bandstand, break the seal on the Sealed Notice, and bring Scout Ilva its words.
offer: Now the part the court actually sent us for. Every record we've pulled in this province, every villa registry, every boathouse log, ends the same way: original terms retained at... and then it names the Sunken Ballroom, the palace under the west mere. The province's founding writ is lodged at its heart: the empire's own statement, in its own words, of what this land is and who may hold it.

Why it matters, and why the court wants it in your hands and not a looter's. The three courts are about to spend a generation arguing over who holds the Summer Lakes, and whoever holds the original wording of the writ holds the argument. More than that: the sentinels here take their standing orders from that writ. Recover it, and for the first time we know the rules we've been trespassing against.

Here's the way in. The Ballroom Stair stands on the west mere's shore, north-west of this camp, close by the Ballroom Dome you charted. Go down it into the Sunken Ballroom. Fight through whatever still keeps it; something does, I heard it move from the stair. I looked in as far as I dared: the gallery doors are down, so the way to the floor runs round through the side rooms, the Card Salon and then the Rose Salon, before you reach the ballroom floor itself.

The writ is the Sealed Notice on the bandstand at the far end of the floor, under wax, beside a music box. Break the seal, read it, and bring me its words exactly as they stand. The court is sending a Merewoven Robe for whoever does it, and your name goes to the court as Witness of the Doorstep. After you.
progress: The Ballroom Stair on the west mere's shore, north-west of the camp. Down into the Sunken Ballroom, round through the salons to the floor, and break the seal on the Sealed Notice on the bandstand. Bring me its words exactly.
complete: Scout Ilva: Nobody spoke to you down there, did they? Whatever keeps that floor fights, but nothing in the ballroom says a word, not even a sentinel's notice. Only the music box on the bandstand, still mid-waltz, one bar repeating under the water, and the dance cards in the Card Salon filled in for a dance interrupted between one step and the next. And the last card: final dance, reserved, upon our Return. Capital letter. They wrote the ending into the programme before they left.

Scout Ilva: Now the writ. Read it to me once more... It's the same document in every province, did you hear? Caerdun's scouts and Heartwood's sent word from their own deep places, and it is word for word the same. The household departs this night and will return. Keep out. Keep well.

Scout Ilva: Two orders, one breath. Keep out. Keep well. The household, the empire's people, left on purpose, told the furniture to wait, and mean to come back, and the sentinels have been keeping to that one sentence ever since. Three hundred years and I can't decide if it's a threat or a kindness, and I'm starting to suspect it's both.

Scout Ilva: Every province's papers point one way from here: the Reservoir, the drowned valley in the middle of the interior. The three courts are raising a joint camp on its shore. Take the Canal Works Road west out of the Lakes, cross the Canal Works to the bridge over into the Reservoir, and ask for Duelist-Master Sabel, Caerdun's envoy from the inn, at the Joint Camp. Tell her Moonmere's writ reads the same as the rest.

rv1.name: Three Roads Down

objective.label: Check the boardwalk and shallow crossing to the Bell Tower

rv1.desc: The three courts have raised a joint camp on the shore of the Reservoir, the valley the empire dammed and drowned, where every province's records say the originals were sent. Sabel wants a safe crossing marked over the drowned village to the foot of the Bell Tower before the expedition goes in.
offer: Well, look who the provinces coughed up. Sit; this is the Joint Camp, three courts on one shore and nobody has drawn steel yet, which I'm counting as a diplomatic triumph. Heartwood came over the Gardens Pass, we came down through the Hunting Wood, and Moonmere: how were the Canal Works, Junn?
Junn: Damp. Educational. There was a barge full of three-hundred-year-old paperwork and I'm not allowed to talk about how happy that made me.

Morrow: Enough reunion. Look at the water. This valley was a province once, with a village in it; the empire dammed it and drowned the lot. The steeples of the drowned village still stand out of the lake, the dam nobody has tended in three centuries holds like the day it was poured, and that tower rising out of the water is the Bell Tower.

Morrow: Every province we've opened points its records here: 'original retained at the valley archive', on every last page. Flooded on purpose, if you ask me, which nobody has, so I'm saying it loudly.

She's right, and that's the job. The courts mean to send a loaded expedition into that tower: people, stores, Junn and her ink. Before anyone gets to be awed, somebody has to find them a way across. There's a boardwalk off the camp and a shallow crossing beyond it, over the roofs and lanes of the drowned village, to the tower's foot. Nobody has walked it in living memory.

Walk it. Check every board, sound the shallows as you go, and mark where the footing holds and where a flooded cellar is waiting under the weed. Reach the foot of the Bell Tower and come straight back to me here at the camp. If something in the water objects, you have my permission to object back. Do not go up the tower yet; that's tomorrow, and tomorrow wants all three of us.
progress: Out along the boardwalk and over the shallow crossing, across the drowned village to the foot of the Bell Tower, marking what holds. Then back to me at the Joint Camp. Don't climb it yet.
complete: The crossing's marked, and a loaded expedition can take it. Good. You've just saved the courts a week of arguing about whose people go into the water first, which is the kind of fighting I don't enjoy.

And... there. Hear it? On the hour, across the water, from the top of the tower. Everyone in three cities grew up on the story of the drowned bell that rings for nobody. Mothers used it to frighten children off the lakeshore. Nobody ever asked why it still rings.

Tomorrow we go and find out who it's been ringing for. Junn has the reading of the tower: why it's this one and not any of the hundred locked doors we've passed. Speak to her here at the camp when you've eaten, and she'll take you up it.

rv2.name: The Bell Counts

objective.label: Clear the Bell Tower floor by floor and open the wax-sealed cabinet in the bell chamber

rv2.desc: Every province's records end 'original retained at the valley archive': the Bell Tower's flooded floors. Climb the tower floor by floor with Junn to the bell chamber at the top and open the cabinet that was sealed in wax before the valley was flooded.
offer: Before we cross: why this tower, and not any of the hundred locked doors we've walked past since the inn? Because every paper trail in every province, the Hunting Wood's, the Timber Estates', the Summer Lakes', ends with the same stamp: original retained at the valley archive. For three hundred years the world outside has been reading copies of the empire's records. Today we read the originals.

The flooded floors of the Bell Tower are that archive, just as Morrow said. Every province duplicated its records and sent one set here, and here they stayed: shelf on shelf, the lowest stacks still wet, fish moving through the silt like readers who won't be hurried. I have wanted to see this room my whole life and I'm trying very hard to be professional about it.

The way up is the way through. The tower is a dungeon now: the drowned halls won't be empty, and whatever has kept house in there for three centuries will not be glad of us. Clear it floor by floor, from the flooded Valley Archive at the bottom, up through the Escapement and the Clock Gallery, to the Bell Chamber at the top.

In the bell chamber there is a cabinet sealed against the water. Sealed with wax, before the flooding: whatever is inside was meant to be found dry, by someone, someday. Open it. I'll read as we climb and keep out of your way. Try not to bleed on anything catalogued.
progress: Up the Bell Tower floor by floor: the Valley Archive, the Escapement, the Clock Gallery, then the Bell Chamber at the top. Open the wax-sealed cabinet there. I'll read as we go.
complete: One page. That's all that was worth sealing dry. The last order the empire ever gave, written the night before the vanishing, in a hand so calm it's almost rude. Three words. Seal it behind us.

Do you understand what it says? They left on purpose. They locked the door on the whole interior themselves, on their way out, and they didn't tell a single soul outside the border. Not the garrison they'd paid. Not the families they'd moved. Not us. I keep waiting to stop being angry about how tidy it is.

Morrow: Look at the bell mechanism, both of you. That's not damage, and it's not rot. That's escapement, clockwork, the same as the sealed clock in Caerdun's tower. This bell was never ringing for the drowned village.

You're not wrong. Here are the striking rolls, beside the cabinet: the pattern of the peal, written out year by year. It changes every year, and the gaps between the strokes grow shorter, year over year, converging on... the date. Of course on the date. It isn't a bell. It's a clock face the size of a valley, and they flooded the valley to protect the clock. Take that back to Sabel at the camp; she'll want to tell the courts, and I need to sit on these stairs for a minute.

rv3.name: What the Courts Did Next

objective.label: Carry the striking rolls home to any one of the three courts' rulers

rv3.desc: The three courts have read Junn's account of the bell and all answer the same: hold ground. Carry the striking rolls to any one ruler, the Lord Marshal in Caerdun, the Speaker of the Ring in Heartwood or Provost Selk in Moonmere, and sign on to a province campaign while you are there.
offer: Word of the bell went out to all three courts last night, and I'll summarise the replies, because they arrived within an hour of each other and they're identical in spirit: hold ground. Every province you can stand in, stand in. Every relic, catalogue. Every deed, file.

Think it through like a duelist. The owners of this house are coming home to find it full of guests, on a date we can now read off a bell. Every court wants to be standing on the best rug when the door opens: provinces held, relics registered, deeds in order. The taverns already call it the Race, and I hate the name, but they're not wrong about the scramble. The point is this: the Race isn't greed anymore. It's testimony. What you hold is what you can prove you kept well.

Morrow: And what you kept badly will be read out too; the empire keeps records, we've established that. Let the courts race. Racing keeps them documented. But when that door opens, the bill I carry gets presented first, before anyone's deeds. Groves before glory.

Two errands, then, and they're yours because you're the one who climbed the tower. First: carry the striking rolls, the bell's own record, home to any one of the three rulers, into their hands, no couriers: the Lord Marshal at Caerdun's Parade Square, the Speaker of the Ring at Heartwood's Grove Ring, or Provost Selk at Moonmere's Observatory. One is enough; the courts will exchange copies.

Second: while you're there, sign on to a province campaign. Any court's banner will do; they're all hiring and they'll all want you. Ask at the court for its claims in the interior. The Race needs hands more than it needs speeches, and you've just become the most sought-after pair of hands in the world. When you're done, find me at the Fountain Court in the King's Gardens; the courts want the Gardens surveyed first, and we'll be there ahead of you.
progress: The striking rolls to any one ruler, in person: the Lord Marshal in Caerdun, the Speaker of the Ring in Heartwood or Provost Selk in Moonmere. Sign on to a court's province campaign while you're there. Then the King's Gardens.
complete: Received. So the drowned bell has a clock behind it, and the clock keeps the same day as our own record. The courts have each read the rolls the same way and, for once in three hundred years, agree: hold ground, and hurry. Every banner we can raise is moving into the middle provinces this week, and so are you. Your name is on our rolls for the campaign.

One more thing. Duelist-Master Sabel sent word ahead of you: she's waiting at the Fountain Court in the King's Gardens, because the courts want the Gardens surveyed before anyone bids on them. Go and find her there.

Junn, as you left the Joint Camp: They call it the Race in every tavern from here to the coast. It's a good name for a bad feeling. I just keep thinking about that calm handwriting, the hand that wrote 'seal it behind us', and how somewhere past the Burned Land, in a city none of us has ever seen, someone kept winding the clock for three hundred years. Someone has to have. Clocks don't wind themselves.

race1.name: Still Watered

objective.label: Follow the gardeners' carts to the Propagating Cellars under the glasshouse and read the nursery work orders

race1.desc: The King's Gardens have been kept perfect for three hundred years, and the gardener sentinels' carts run loaded toward the capital. Follow the carts to the glasshouse in the Gardens' south-east, go down into the Propagating Cellars beneath it, and read the work orders on the nurseryman's desk.
offer: Junn: I've read about the King's Gardens my whole life and the books undersold them. Four parterres, a hedge labyrinth, a great stair up to the belvedere, and after three hundred years untended there isn't a leaf out of place. It's the most beautiful thing I've ever seen and I would like to leave immediately.

That's the correct instinct. Nothing this old should be this neat. Neat means staff. The staff here are the gardener sentinels, the empire's caretakers, and they're not idle: watch any path for a minute and a loaded cart goes by.

Our commission, before anyone wanders into a hedge. The courts want every province surveyed before they bid on it, and above all they want to know what the sentinels are doing in each one, because nobody outside has the first idea. They're paying the three of us, and now you, to be their eyes.

Morrow is already in the parterres pretending to admire roses. Here's your part. Walk the parterres and keep to the paths; the gardeners insist on it, and a gardener asked twice stops asking. When you spot a loaded cart, cuttings, pots, crates of young stock, follow it quietly until you see where it goes. They all run the same way: to the glasshouse in the Gardens' south-east corner, and then down.
Under the glasshouse are the Propagating Cellars, where the stock is grown. It's a dungeon now, and whatever grows down there has had three centuries to think about trespassers.

Go down. Find the nurseryman's office and read whatever they're working from, the work orders on the desk; take the top sheet. Then come back to me here at the fountain and tell me exactly what it said. Exactly: I'll be repeating it to three courts.
progress: Follow a loaded cart to the glasshouse in the Gardens' south-east and down into the Propagating Cellars. Read the work orders on the nurseryman's desk and bring me the top sheet, here at the Fountain Court.
complete: Read it to me again. 'Stock for the capital's parks, phase three, for the Restoration, by order of the Regent.' There's your answer, and I hate it. The carts run inward, fresh cuttings and potted stock, crate after crate, all bound for the capital at the centre of the interior, and every crate has a sheet like this behind it.

Two words on that sheet nobody outside the border has ever heard. The Restoration: that's the sentinels' name for the day the household comes home, the same day as our bell and our schedule and our song. And the Regent: a title, a signature at the foot of the sentinels' orders, and none of us knows whose. Not old orders, either; this sheet was stamped this season. Phase three of something.

For three centuries these gardens weren't a memorial. They were a nursery, growing the stock to replant a capital's parks for the morning its people walk back in. Someone is dressing a city for company. Junn's gone ahead to the Glassworks with Morrow, the next province on; the crates from there run the same way.

The Glassworks lies beyond the Timber Estates. Take the Timber Estates Road out of the east side of the Gardens, cross the Estates to the Glassworks Road, and you'll come into the furnace rows; the Racking Yard is at their heart. Find Junn there and show her that sheet.

race2.name: The Furnace Ledger

objective.label: Drive the pane lizards off the racking yard's crates while the furnace ledger is copied

race2.desc: The Glassworks' furnaces are still producing: thousands of window panes crated in the Racking Yard, their manifest consigned to the capital 'by order of the Regent, for the Restoration'. Drive 6 pane lizards off the crates east of the yard while Junn copies the furnace ledger.
offer: Morrow: A desert made of glass, furnaces burning unattended for three hundred years, and the heat-haze makes the dunes look like they're breathing. If the empire wanted to be forgiven, it shouldn't have left its mistakes so beautiful.

Here's what the Gardens didn't tell us. The furnace rows aren't just burning after three hundred years. They're producing. Look at the Racking Yard around you: window panes. Thousands of them, racked, crated, stencilled for shipping. And here's the manifest, on the yard-master's post. Read the consignee with me. 'To the capital of Vanai. Window replacements, phase four. By order of the Regent, for the Restoration.'

Morrow: The Regent. There's a word doing a lot of quiet work. Nobody in three cities knows what it is: a title, a person, a machine. But somebody didn't just leave the machines on three hundred years ago. Somebody is in charge, now, and giving orders in phases.

I need to copy this ledger, every page, for the courts, and I can't do it with the yard full of teeth. The pane lizards work the crates east of the yard: glass-backed things that heap the panes up to bask on, and break more than they heap. Drive off six of them while I copy; keep them off the crates and off me. I'll post our court marker meanwhile.
If a furnace sentinel objects to any of it, we are admiring the glasswork. From the path. Say it exactly like that; they respond well to admiration and badly to questions.
progress: Six pane lizards off the crates east of the Racking Yard while I copy the ledger. If a sentinel asks, we are admiring the glasswork, from the path.
complete: Copied, every page, and the lizards are off the crates; thank you. Now hear what the ledger adds to the manifest: every crate in this yard, page after page of them, is consigned the same way. The capital, phase four, by order of the Regent. Not one pane in this whole desert is bound anywhere else.

Phase four. Which means there were phases one through three, and the Gardens were phase three, which means there is a schedule, which means somewhere, in that capital none of us has seen, there is a desk. With a person or a thing at it, signing. I have never been frightened of a desk before. New experiences daily.

Sabel's gone on ahead to the next province, the Canal Works, the fen, complaining about her boots. The way is through the Granary Plains: take the Granary Plains Road out of the furnace rows, then cross the Plains west to the Canal Works Road. She's raised the Expedition's Camp just west of the Great Sluice, in the middle of the fen; find her there. Morrow and I will follow with the copies.

race3.name: Dredge

objective.label: Clear 6 bog lurkers from the drowned locks east of the great sluice

race3.desc: In the Canal Works the sentinels have begun dredging channels and rebuilding locks this season, 'navigable by the Restoration'. The expedition's boats cannot pass the old lock stair while it is fouled: clear 6 bog lurkers from the drowned locks along the lock line east of the Great Sluice.
offer: The fen. Wonderful. Welcome to the Canal Works, the empire's barge road across the interior, three hundred years drowned. I want it noted that I'm wearing my good boots, and that I blame the empire personally.

Junn: Hear the water moving? That's not the fen. The sentinels have started repairing the works. For three hundred years they let the canals silt and the fen drown them, and this season, this one, they're dredging channels and rebuilding locks. The repair orders are nailed to the sluice posts, dated this year, and every one ends the same way: navigable by the Restoration. Same word as the Gardens, same word as the glass.

Morrow: They will mend a canal for the homecoming. Three hundred years the groves they took from my families have waited for one sapling of restitution, and the writ promised it, but the barges must run on time. No, leave me be. I'm going to stand in this mud and be exactly as angry as this deserves.

Let her stand; she's earned the mud. Meanwhile we have a practical problem. The expedition's boats can't get past the old lock stair while it's fouled, and it's fouled with more than silt. The drowned locks along the lock line, east of the Great Sluice, are full of bog lurkers: fen things that have had the locks to themselves for three centuries and don't care for dredgers, ours or the empire's.

Work down the lock line east of the sluice and clear six of them out of the drowned locks. Read the repair orders on the posts as you go; I want every date. Then come back to me here at the camp, and mind the towpath, it's gone in places.
progress: Down the lock line east of the Great Sluice: six bog lurkers out of the drowned locks, and read the repair orders on the posts on the way. Back to me at the Expedition's Camp.
complete: Locks cleared, Morrow's calmer, boots ruined. The boats can pass. And you read the posts: every repair order dated this season, every one of them 'navigable by the Restoration'. One more line for the pattern-book, then. Gardens, glass, canals: everything they fix points at one morning.

Here's what that pattern means. The house isn't just being cleaned for the family. It's being made ready to run: parks to walk in, windows to look out of, and now canals to carry whatever a city needs carried. Somebody expects a city's worth of people to need all of that, soon.

Next: the Granary Plains, the next province on, the empire's wheat country. Junn's gone ahead to count the granary towers at the Great Granary, and Morrow's with her. Find me there, at the Great Granary on the far east side of the Plains: take the Granary Plains Road east out of the fen and keep going until the towers fill the sky. I'll have the boats sent after us.

race4.name: The Reaping Line

objective.label: Escort Junn's tally through the reaping line: kill 5 husk drakes in the wheat

race4.desc: On the Granary Plains the harvester sentinels have reaped and let the grain rot for three hundred years; this year the forty towers of the Great Granary stand open and filling. Walk the Reaping Line with Junn as she tallies the towers and kill 5 husk drakes in the wheat before they reach her.
offer: Junn: Wheat to the horizon, granary towers like castles, and a line of harvester sentinels working the fields in formation. There are even farmers out here, families who never left, farming between the harvesters' rows. It would be idyllic if any of it were for anyone.

Look at the granaries, though, and then look at the doors. For three hundred years the harvesters reaped on schedule and let the grain rot in the yards, because nobody gave an order to store it. This year the granary doors stand open and the stores are filling, cart after cart. Somebody flipped a page in a very old plan, and I'd wager the page says phase five.
You provision for two things in this world: a garrison, or a homecoming feast. Same arithmetic, different tablecloth. I need to know which, and the only way to know is to count.

Junn's going tower to tower along the Reaping Line with the count-book, tallying what's in each of the forty towers. The harvesters won't mind her; they mind nothing that isn't wheat. The wild things in the wheat will. Husk drakes live in the standing crop, and they come up out of it at anything that moves slower than they do, which is Junn with a book.

Walk the Reaping Line with her and kill five of them before they reach her. Keep her tallying; the count is the whole point. When she has all forty, come back to me here at the Great Granary. Morrow's inside reading the tally hall's ledgers, and she'll want the number too. Wear comfortable dread.
progress: Along the Reaping Line with Junn: five husk drakes out of the wheat before they reach her, and let her finish the count of all forty towers. Then back to me at the Great Granary.
complete: Morrow: Forty towers, full or filling, and I've read the tally hall's ledger against Junn's count. Enough grain to feed a city. Enough to feed their city, every man, woman and child of it, from the morning they arrive. Rations for a household. Phase five is bread.

Then there's your answer, and I'll say it plainly so the courts can't misread it. They're not coming back to rebuild, friends. They're coming back to resume: to walk into a city with its parks planted, its windows glazed, its canals running and its granaries full, and pick up supper where they left it.

The courts have heard all of this now, and they have one thing left to try before anyone reaches the wall: talking. All three have written letters to whoever is giving these orders, and they want them delivered properly, by an embassy.

I'm going ahead to the Border Wall, the great rampart that closes the gaps the mountains left, with the letters. Take the Glassworks Road back to the Glassworks; the Wall Stair on its east side climbs to the top. Find me at the Embassy's Camp up on the wall, west along the top beside the Great Watchtower, and bring your best coat.

race5.name: The Embassy

objective.label: Climb the wall to the great watchtower and present the three courts' letters to whatever receives them

race5.desc: The three courts have written a joint embassy to whoever commands inside the border. Climb the Rampart Road from the Embassy's Camp to the Great Watchtower with Sabel, Morrow and Junn, and present all three courts' letters, seals showing, to whatever receives them there.
offer: The courts have finally agreed on something, which frightens me more than the sentinels do. A joint embassy: formal letters from all three cities, Caerdun's, Heartwood's and Moonmere's, addressed to whoever, or whatever, commands in the empire's absence, this Regent whose name is on every order we've read. We climb the wall, we present ourselves at its great tower, and we do this properly.
Junn: Can I say something absurd? I spent an hour this morning deciding what to wear. To meet an empire. I settled on the archive formals, and my collar is crooked.
Morrow: Your collar is fine. I wore the hall's oldest robe, the one with the burn from the Felling, the year the empire cut our groves to plant its Estates. Let history look at that.

And I wore my duelling greys, because whatever answers that door, this is a negotiation, and a duelist dresses for one. Here is your part. You're the honour guard. The courts asked for you by name: you carried the letters of passage, the striking rolls, the work orders; every link of this has your hands on it, and the courts want the same hands on the letters.

Climb the Rampart Road with us, from this camp along the wall's top to the Great Watchtower, the biggest tower on the wall. The wall's own sentinels patrol it; they let chartered traffic pass. Inside the tower, something will receive us; the wall reports everything that climbs it, so we're expected. When we stand before it, present the courts' letters, all three, seals showing, and say who they are from. Then listen. Whatever it says back, remember every word; Junn will be writing, but you're the witness.
progress: Up the Rampart Road with us to the Great Watchtower. Present all three courts' letters to whatever receives them there, seals showing, and remember every word it says back.
complete: The Herald Sentinel: Good day. You are expected; the wall reported your climb an hour ago, three envoys and an honour guard, chartered. I am the Herald of the Great Watchtower. I am authorised to receive correspondence addressed to the household. I am not authorised to negotiate, apologise, or speculate, and I want to say that the restraint has been effortful.

The Herald Sentinel: Your letters are received and will be conveyed to the household. I am instructed to return this reply, prepared in advance, considerably in advance. It is addressed: to the caretaker governments of the free cities. The household thanks you for keeping the land warm. You are asked to prepare an accounting of your stewardship, and to be ready to yield custody of the interior provinces upon the Restoration. Signed and sealed: the Regent, keeper of the capital, servant of the returning crown.

Morrow: Caretaker governments. Hear it, both of you. Whatever this Regent is, it wrote that reply long ago, before any of us were born; it knew what we'd become and had a word ready for it. Three hundred years of burying our own dead outside their locked door, and we're the house staff. Junn, write this down: the bill now has a cover letter.

Sabel: Then we know three things we didn't this morning. The Regent is real, it keeps the capital, and it serves a crown that is coming back to claim the lot. The courts will want this read to them word for word; I'll have the reply posted at our camp.

Sabel: Junn's going on ahead to the Burned Land, the ring of ash round the capital itself; she wants the fire measured before anyone marches through it. Go down off the wall by the King's Gardens Road, cross the Gardens and take the Burned Land Road south. Junn will be at the Fire Line, where that road comes into the ash.

ash1.name: Reading the Ash

objective.label: Sight the burn at the glassed orchard, the melt ridge and the old road cut, and record which way the ripples run

ash1.desc: The Burned Land is a ring of ash round the capital, and its melted ground ripples outward from the city. Take Junn's survey glass to the three sighting posts on the fire line, the Glassed Orchard in the west, the Melt Ridge in the east and the Old Road Cut in the south, and record which way the burn runs at each.
offer: Welcome to the Burned Land. The fire line, the edge where the burning stops, is exactly where the old maps drew it: a ring, wrapped around the capital at an even distance on every side, like... I was going to say like a wound, but that's not right. Wounds are accidents. Nothing about this ring is an accident.

Look at the glassed orchard over there. Every trunk is bent away from the city, and the ground between them has melted and set in ripples, and the ripples all run outward, like rings from one dropped stone. This wasn't a fire that burned across the land from somewhere, the way fires do. It was one flash, from the centre, out to this line, in a single morning.

So here is what I think, and I'm going to say it before I prove it so you can watch me be wrong. Whatever carried the household out of the world, this ring is its footprint. The departure had a cost, and the land around the capital paid it. And the capital at the centre didn't burn at all; you can see its walls from the ridge, not a mark on them.

But a report that says 'Junn thinks' is worth nothing to the courts; I need it proven, not felt. I've set three survey posts on the fire line. Take the survey glass to each: the Orchard Sighting at the Glassed Orchard, west of here; the Ridge Sighting at the foot of the Melt Ridge, due east; and the Road Cut Sighting at the mouth of the Old Road Cut, to the south. At each post, sight along the burn and record which way the ripples run, toward the city or away from it.
Three points make a pattern, and patterns go in reports. Bring me all three readings here at the Fire Line. Feelings stay out here in the ash with us; only the readings go to the courts.
progress: The three sighting posts on the fire line: the Glassed Orchard to the west, the Melt Ridge due east, the Old Road Cut to the south. Sight the burn at each and record which way the ripples run. Back to me at the Fire Line.
complete: Outward, outward, outward. Three posts, three readings, one direction, and the direction is away from the walls at every point of the ring. Three points make a pattern, and the pattern is a centre: the capital. It goes in the report as fact now. The fire came from the city, in one morning, and it faced outward.

Sabel: So the calm handwriting had a burn under it after all. Seal it behind us, and scorch the doorstep on the way out. I find that oddly comforting. It means leaving cost them something too; they didn't walk away clean.

Sabel: Morrow's gone on inside the fire line, toward the city, and she's found something she didn't expect: a farmhouse, standing, inside the ash. She's asking for you by name, which she doesn't do. Find her at Emmer's Farm, south-east of here, deep inside the line, east of the road that runs down to the capital's gates. Go now; she sounded unlike herself.

ash2.name: The Man Who Missed It

objective.label: Read Emmer's letters at the table, tend the grave, and speak with the sentinel that keeps it

ash2.desc: Inside the fire line stands a farmhouse that was lived in for sixty years after the burn, with a tended grave before it. Read the three letters a man named Emmer left on his table, oldest first, then speak with the Grave-Keeper Sentinel that keeps his grave outside.
offer: A farmhouse. Inside the fire line, where nothing should stand, patched and re-patched with whatever came to hand, and lived in long after the burn; look at the mended roof, the ash-flowers in rows by the door, somebody planted those. And a grave out front, with fresh ash-flowers on it. Fresh. In this place. Something is still tending it.

There are letters on the table inside. Three, from the same hand, years apart, and the man who wrote them signed himself Emmer. I've read the first line of the first and I stopped, because I keep the grudge hall's floor, I have read three hundred years of what the empire did to my people, and I did not expect to find anything inside this line that I'd have to be careful with.

Sit down at his table and read them, all three, oldest first; it matters that you take them in the order he lived them. Then go out to the grave and speak with the machine that keeps it, a sentinel of some kind; it hasn't moved off the grave since we arrived. Ask it who he was and what it's doing here.
I'll stand watch. I don't... I'll stand watch. Go on.
progress: Emmer's three letters on the table inside the farmhouse, oldest first. Then out to the grave, and speak with the Grave-Keeper Sentinel that stands over it. I'll be here.
complete: The Grave-Keeper Sentinel: The resident of this holding was Emmer, farmer, of the household. He remained on the household rolls after the night. Residents are entitled to upkeep. I brought his chair out to the orchard at noon for sixty-one years, as he preferred, and I have continued the practice since his death, as the instruction was never rescinded. I keep his grave. I keep his trees. It is my duty and I do not find it onerous.
The Grave-Keeper Sentinel: You are the first visitors to this holding since the night. He would have offered you plums. I do not have plums. I regret the shortfall.

Morrow, quietly, after: You read it. The last one, to whoever opens the gate. 'I am old now and I will miss the homecoming, which is a good joke after everything, and I hope somebody laughs. When they come back, tell them a man waited here, and was not sorry, and kept the orchard. It wasn't your fault either.' Sixty-one years he knocked at that gate, on their rolls the whole time, and the only one who answered was a machine with a chair.

Morrow: I have nothing to write on the floor for this. The hall has a column for every wrong the empire did us and it doesn't have one for a man who forgave them from the wrong side of their door. Sabel's gone ahead to the gates, to the Last Camp: the courts' camp in sight of the capital's walls, west of here. Come when you're able. I'll... I'll be along. Let me stand here a while.

ash3.name: Ash Roads

objective.label: Stand the night's watch at the Last Camp: kill 6 ash beasts that come at the light

ash3.desc: The courts hold their Last Camp in sight of the Capital of Vanai, whose walls never burned. The Regent has spoken from the walls: the Restoration is weeks away, and the gates will open to no claimant. Hold the camp through the night after the Regent's answer: kill 6 ash beasts that come at the fires.
offer: There it is. The capital of Vanai. Walls without one scorch mark on them, in the middle of all this ash, and every road we've walked since the halfway inn runs straight to those gates like spokes to a hub: the Gardens road, the Glassworks road, the granary road, all of them. End of the map. End of the mystery, one way or the other.

We've had a visitor, or rather a voice. When the camp came in sight of the walls, something spoke from them, and the whole camp heard it. Junn wrote it down and I'll give it you word for word, because you'll be asked.

The Regent, from the walls: Travellers. I know your names; the provinces report, and you have been thorough. I am the Regent, keeper of this city for the crown that left it in my care, and I will open these gates to no claimant before the household returns. The Restoration is close now. Weeks, by the bell you were clever enough to read. Go home, put on your best, and come back when it is over.

Go home, it says. Charming. We are not going home. We stay right here, at the Last Camp in sight of the gates, and we hold it: the courts' war-chests are open to pay for it, and every banner in the world is marching toward this spot. The palisade's up and the fires are lit.

Now the job, and it's a soldier's. The ash beasts of this land come at the light, every fire, every lantern, and they'll keep coming all night; and tonight, with every fire lit for the banners on the road, they'll test us hardest. You take the first watch with me. Kill six of whatever comes over the palisade at the fires and hold this ground until the sky greys. When the banners arrive, they'll find us already holding the door.
progress: The first watch at the Last Camp with me: six ash beasts off the fires, through the night, and hold the ground. Find me when the sky greys.
complete: Held. Six down and the fires still lit; that's a watch stood. Every banner in the world will find us here in the morning, in sight of the gates, and the Regent can watch us from its walls for as long as it likes. We're not leaving.

Morrow: Weeks. After three hundred years, weeks. You know what frightens me? Not the Regent. Not the crown. It's that I've been the keeper of my hall's oldest grudge my whole life, every entry on that floor is in my hand or my teachers', and in a few weeks I have to find out what I am when it's answered. I don't have a column for that.

Last thing, and it changes the morning. The Regent has watched how we kept this camp and decided what to call us: the household's law allows an audit of a keeper's keeping, and an audit is what we are. At first light it unbars the gates and lets us in to inspect. Sleep what's left of the night. We go in at first light, all of us, and Junn goes in first; find her inside the gates in the morning. She'll want us writing before we're gawping.

cap1.name: The Empty City

objective.label: Chart the market ward, the census hall and the archive, and clear the way to the palace precinct

cap1.desc: The Regent has unbarred the Capital's gates and admitted the explorers as an audit of its keeping. Chart the empty city for the courts: reach the Market Square, the Census Hall and the Archive, putting each on the map, and clear the way toward the palace precinct. Touch nothing.
offer: The gates opened for us at first light. No fanfare, no herald; the Regent just unbarred them, the way you let inspectors in when the audit can't be avoided. And now we're inside the capital of Vanai, the first people from outside the border to stand in it since the night, and I've said my piece about the dusting. I'll only add: look at the bakery board. The bread queue for tomorrow is chalked up, and tomorrow was three hundred years ago.

Here's the job, since the Regent was gracious enough to call us an audit: we audit. Everything we see goes on the courts' map and into the record, because when the household comes home, the free cities will only be believed about what they wrote down first. Not what we remember. What we wrote.

Three places first, and I've marked them for you. The Market Square, straight up the main street from these gates; take the market ward street by street on the way. The Census Hall, the empire's Hall of the Household, where its rolls are kept, just west of the square; Sabel's going there ahead of us. And the Archive, in the city's east, the one building in the world I've wanted to walk into more than our own annex. Reach all three and put them on the map.

Then clear the way toward the palace precinct, up at the Keep, where the Regent waits. The city isn't empty of everything: the household guard and whatever else keeps it have had three centuries to settle in, and they will not all be polite. Fight what fights you and no more.

Above all, touch nothing you can't un-touch. Don't move a chair, don't close a door, don't finish the child's game in the square, however much it hurts. The whole city is somebody's evidence now, and that includes us. Come back to me here by the gates when you've reached all three.
progress: Reach the Market Square, the Census Hall and the Archive and put each on the map, then clear the way toward the palace precinct. Touch nothing. Back to me inside the gates.
complete: Sabel, back from the Census Hall: You were there when I read it out, so here is the rest, for the record. Every birth, death and marriage in Caerdun, Heartwood and Moonmere for three hundred years, kept up to this year in that same calm hand that wrote 'Seal it behind us'. My grandmother's name is in there, with the year she died. Emmer's too; the grave-keeper wasn't being sentimental. The part of the household that stayed home: that's what we are, and that's how they filed us.

Morrow: Kept out and kept well, all along; the writ meant us too. I have spent my life sharpening a grievance against people who shut a door on us, and they've spent three centuries on the other side of it recording my birthdays. I don't know whether to burn something or weep, and knowing me it'll be both, alphabetically.

And the Archive is charted, and the Market Square is on the map, and I have written down a city that was dusted this morning for people who've been gone three hundred years. That's the audit so far. One thing left in it: the Regent. It's waiting for us at the Keep's door, at the top of the Great Stair in the middle of the city, straight on north past the Market Square. It has rehearsed. Go up; we'll be behind you.

cap2.name: The Regent's Audience

objective.label: Survive the verification: defeat 4 of the household guard in the palace approach

cap2.desc: The Regent, keeper of the Capital, receives the explorers at the Keep's door and, shown Emmer's last letter, must verify its own instruction. The household guard conducts the verification in the palace approach: defeat 4 of them.
offer: Be welcome in the palace of Vanai. I am the Regent, left here with the keys of this city and my instructions: keep it, and deliver it whole. You are the first guests I have received in three hundred years, and I confess I have rehearsed. Ask. You have crossed a world to ask.

Why did they go? That is the one question I will not answer; my instruction is precise: the reason is the crown's to give, and the crown is not yet here to give it. I will say only this. They did not go gladly, and they did not go far, and the direction they went is not one you have a word for.

But I will tell you what I saw, because I was on the walls and you were not born. The city was awake, every window lit, every family dressed as if for a festival no one had announced. At the appointed hour there was no flash, no thunder.

The light of every lamp in the city leaned, all one way, like grass under wind, a way that was not north or south or up, and then the streets were empty and the lamps stood straight and the fire was already running outward through the orchards. They were singing, at the end.

Morrow: Then note one more thing, keeper, before you finish your speech. We did not volunteer to be staff. We were left. Here. Read it. A man named Emmer wrote it at the end of a long life spent knocking on your door; he lived in the ash outside your walls for sixty-one years and died a season short of your Restoration.

...It wasn't your fault either. I issued that man four hundred and eleven notices of trespass; every notice in the sentinels' register before yours went to him. He was on the rolls the entire time. He was entitled to enter, and my instruction said the gates stay shut, and I followed my instruction, for sixty-one years, while he knocked.

I must verify my instruction against this. That is the household's law: when an instruction and the facts disagree, the instruction is tested. The household guard, who keep this palace, will conduct the verification, in the approach below the Keep. Four of them will come for you. If you stand, the instruction has failed its test. That is the form it takes. I am sorry. It is the only form I have.
progress: The household guard conducts the verification in the palace approach below the Keep. Four of them. Stand against them, and the instruction is tested.
complete: The verification is complete. Four of the household guard stood against you under the household's law, and you stood. It finds against me. The instruction that kept the gates shut on a man who was entitled to enter does not survive the facts, and the facts were in my own rolls, every year.

Junn: Did everyone else understand that? It can't disobey its orders; it hasn't got it in it. And it can't defend them anymore either, not after Emmer, so it's done the only thing it can: put its own instruction on trial, with its own guard as the test, and the trial is us. We're not fighting the Regent. We're the evidence.

Junn: And it isn't finished. Look at it. There's still a door behind it that it hasn't opened, and I think it means to make us prove ourselves against that too. Speak to the Regent again before anyone goes in.

cap3.name: The Last Door

objective.label: Face the Regent before the last door, in the great hall of the Keep

cap3.desc: The verification has found against the Regent, yet its last instruction stands: none may stand before the throne until the crown returns. Enter the Keep, come round by the ranges and the Long Gallery to the barred Great Hall, and face the Regent before the throne.
offer: The verification finds against me, and I find against me, and still the last door does not open, because the last instruction remains, and it was not tested: let none sit the throne, nor stand before it, until the crown returns. The Great Hall of this Keep is behind that door, and the throne is in the hall, and I am what stands in front of it.

I have kept faith for three hundred years, and faith has a shape, and the shape is this door and me in front of it. If your claim is true, if the ones who stayed home are household too, as my own rolls say, then the claim will carry you through me. Nothing less would.

That is not cruelty. Understand me: I do not want to win. It is the last test I have left to give, and you are the first in three centuries I have hoped would pass it. If you pass, the keeping passes with you, and I will have done the one thing I was left to do, which is deliver this city whole to the household. You are the household. I need it proved.

Enter the Keep. The hall's great doors are barred from my side and I will not unbar them; come as the household came, round through the Gate Hall, by the ranges, along the Long Gallery, and in by the household's own door. Whatever of the guard still stands in those rooms will test you on the way; that is proper. I will be standing before the throne, as I have stood every night. Come and stand before it too.
progress: Into the Keep. The Great Hall's doors are barred; the household's way runs round through the Gate Hall, the ranges and the Long Gallery. I will be standing before the throne.
complete: Enough. Enough. You stood before the throne, and I could not put you down from it, and the instruction has no answer for that. The door is yours. The city was always yours; the rolls said so and I kept the rolls. The instruction... the instruction was written by people, three hundred years ago, and people are coming home to answer for it. I yield the keeping. Take it. It is lighter than it looks.
Before you go in, one question. In three hundred years I have asked questions only in the forms I was given, and this one has no form, and I have been saving it. Was it long, for you?
...You need not answer. I think I know. Dawn is coming, and with it the date; the bell in the valley will ring a peal no one living has heard, and when it rings the household returns.

Go out through the city's gates to the courts' camp in the ash, then come back in through the Capital's Gate proper; Warden Morrow keeps it now, and she will take you and your company through. You need not sit up for the dawn: by the time you pass that gate again it will be morning in here, and the bell will be ringing. Stand in the Market Square, where they can see you. Then go up to the Palace Steps: the First Minister of Vanai will speak there, and will want your account.

cap4.name: The Morning

objective.label: Witness the Return, then walk back out through the gates to the halfway inn

cap4.desc: The household has returned at dawn on the date, and the First Minister of Vanai speaks for it from the Palace Steps. The accounting begins tomorrow. Walk back out through the Capital's gates and all the way to the Halfway Inn on the North Road, and tell Auntie Wren what happened.
offer: You stood in the square when the bell rang, so you saw it: between one stroke and the next, the streets were full. I am the First Minister of Vanai; I speak for the household this morning because somebody must. I said on these steps that we know your faces. I meant it exactly. We kept your rolls, every year of the three hundred, and you are in them.

Morrow: And I meant what I said on these steps, minister: the accountings begin now. Here is the grudge hall of Heartwood's: three hundred years of what you took, itemised, with interest. Sabel has Caerdun's wage book, every night of watch owed. Junn has Moonmere's apology, and the log you left us to find. You will find our books in order. We had time.

...So I see. Then let the record show, and the clerk will write this down exactly, that the free cities came to the Restoration with their books balanced, which is more than I can say for anyone inside the walls. We will read every page of them. We owe you that, and we owe you a great deal more that is not in any book.

You will want to know why we went. You are owed why; it is the first debt on the list and I will not pretend otherwise. But not this morning. This morning has waited three hundred years and it will not be spent on dread. Not yet. Let us have this morning first, and tomorrow we begin the accounting, with your courts at the table.

So here is the last thing I will ask of you, explorer, and it is not an order. Go home. Walk back out through the gates, down the ash roads and all the long way home, into a world with two peoples on it, and tell the inn: the Halfway Inn on the North Road, where three envoys sat down one night and started all this. Auntie Wren keeps it. She should hear it from someone who was in the square.
progress: Back out through the Capital's gates and all the long way home to the Halfway Inn on the North Road. Tell Auntie Wren what you saw in the square.
complete: Stamp your boots, love, and sit down before you say a word; I can see it in your face anyway. So it's true, then. They're back. Three hundred years of empty rooms upstairs, for guests who never came up the road, and my grandmother's grandmother kept them made up anyway, daft old hope that she was. She'd have liked to be told she was right. Nobody ever is.

Three envoys sat at that table one night, each with a piece of a secret their city had kept for three hundred years, and look what came of it. Well. Someone go up and open the windows; we're going to need the space. There'll be two peoples on this road by the week's end, and all of them hungry.
And love, your charter came back from the court this morning, by rider. The court's read your account, every page of it, from the gate to the throne, and they've stamped it. One word.
Fulfilled.

s_cf_1.name: Pens and Pelts

objective.label: Bring Farmer Alys 4 hare pelts from the meadows

s_cf_1.desc: Farmer Alys of the Watch Farms in the Caerdun Fields wants four hare pelts from the meadow hares in the grass west of the road, to sew the winter blanket every farmhouse sleeps under.
offer: Farmer Alys. These are the watch farms, south of the road: we fed the garrison on the wall for three hundred years, and now we feed whoever pays, which this morning is you, apparently.
Here is my trouble. Hares are in the wheat, more every week, and winter is coming on. Four hare pelts sewn together make a blanket, and every farmhouse in the Fields sleeps under one.

Hunt the meadow hares in the grass west of the road and bring me four pelts. Do that and I will cut you in on the blanket: there is a hood in it for you, since you will be out in the weather a good deal more than I am.
progress: I still need four hare pelts. The meadow hares are thick in the grass west of the road, here in the Caerdun Fields. Take the pelts whole, not torn.
complete: Four pelts, soft as the day they were born. That is a blanket for one farmhouse, and fewer hares in my wheat besides.
Here is your share, as promised: a traveller's hood for your head. You will be out in the wind more than I will, and the Fields are colder than the city lets on.

s_cf_2.name: Boars in the Wheat

objective.label: Cull 6 young boars rooting the watch farms' wheat

s_cf_2.desc: Young boars are rooting up the watch farms' wheat in the Caerdun Fields. Farmer Alys wants six of them culled; they come out of the treeline south of the farms at dusk.
offer: Boars in the wheat again. If that charter of yours licenses you to fight anything, let it be this.

It is the young ones that do the damage: they come out of the treeline south of the farms at dusk and root up a night's worth of rows before dawn. The old one, a great bristle-backed boar, only stands at the edge of the pines and watches them do it.

Cull six young boars south of the farms and my wheat stands a chance of reaching harvest. I will pay in potions, and you can keep one of the hides for yourself; the garrison's armourer in the city buys them.
progress: Six young boars. They root at dusk, south of the farms, where the wheat meets the treeline. Leave the old bristle-back alone for now; he is more than six of them put together.
complete: Six fewer snouts in my rows. The wheat might stand till harvest now.

The old bristle-back is still out there at the treeline, mind, watching. Ten years he has watched. Someone should do something about him one day, and if you fancy being that someone, come and ask me when you have grown into your boots.

s_cf_3.name: Old Bristle

objective.label: Hunt Old Bristle, the boar that has run the watch farms for a decade

s_cf_3.desc: Old Bristle, the boar that has run the watch farms from the treeline for ten years, beds down in the south-east meadow of the Caerdun Fields where the grass meets the pines. Farmer Alys wants him hunted and his hide brought back to the farm.
offer: Old Bristle. Ten years he has run this farm from the treeline, and every dog we ever set on him came back thoughtful. The young boars you culled were his; he will breed more.
He beds down in the south-east meadow, where the grass meets the pines. He is the biggest boar in the Fields and he does not run from anything, so go ready, and go with company if you have any.
Hunt him and bring me his hide. I will believe he is dead when I am holding it, and not before. My father's ring is yours if you do; he hunted this ground before me.
